items.title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
items.content:
TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong.

# Minimal Viable Safety

## The Task

The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do. For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe
[1]
, but also perfectly useless.

We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill
[2]
. However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them.

If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address.

Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS).

## The Problem

Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet
[3]
. It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral
[4]
. It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level.

In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users.

## The Methodology

What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument.

The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems
[5]
, then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them.

In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late.

In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species.

## The Challenge

While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows:

- Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary.

- Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts.

- Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners.

- Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs.

In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish.

# Alignment is Holistic

Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent.

In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs, and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.)

In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s)
[6]
, at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. They need to be beliefs that the user can rationally trust to be accurate. Similarly, "aligned" decision-making needs to be such that the user can rationally trust it to be in their own favor given aligned preferences and beliefs.

The philosophically astute reader will notice that at this point we are already in a world of trouble. What does it mean for the user to have preferences? Are there objectively rational theories of epistemology and decision-making, and if so, what are these theories? Can beliefs or decisions be rational to hold or make "on behalf" of the user even if the user themself doesn't understand why? On the other hand, a computer scientist might be tempted to ignore these difficulties and just forge ahead with a solution that seems pragmatically satisfying. I think there is a lot to be said for such a practical mindset, and in this article I will aspire to embrace it. Unfortunately, we will see that the philosophical difficulties are not easily brushed aside.

Returning to the trichotomy of preferences, beliefs and decisions, observe that it is not even possible to entirely separate the three. For us to ascribe preferences to a system, it must rationally form beliefs and make decisions on the basis of these preferences. For us to ascribe beliefs to a system, it must rationally make decisions on the basis of these beliefs in the context of its preferences. And the rationality of decisions can only be judged in the context of specific preferences and beliefs.

Imagine an AI agent that pursues the happiness of mankind and is irrationally convinced that every human who dies goes to Heaven, which is the best possible place for human happiness. Such an AI would be motivated to kill all humans, even though its preferences are arguably "aligned". Moreover, since the belief in Heaven is unfalsifiable, such an AI can still be extremely capable at acting on its motivation and hence extremely dangerous.

If this thought experiment seems strange, consider the following: our beliefs would seem very strange to people who lived centuries ago. Therefore, it is highly likely that the beliefs of an ASI, capable of intellectual progress much faster than humans, will (and should) quickly become strange to us. The question is whether these strange beliefs will be produced by a process that we should deem trustworthy nevertheless.

"Alignment" is meaningless outside the full context of epistemic and instrumental rationality. Therefore, any theory of alignment has to be, in particular, a theory of epistemic and instrumental rationality.

# Hypercomplexity

Perhaps the most simplistic approach to ensuring that an AI agent has aligned preferences and beliefs is explicitly specifying the preferences and beliefs that the agent should have. However, this is intractable. Human preferences are notoriously complex and giving a precise and complete mathematical specification of them seems hopeless. (Yudkowsky calls this "complexity of value".) It seems no easier to accomplish than identifying images of cats by a handcrafted mathematical specification of "cat".

For weak agents, a practical solution can be explicitly specifying a proxy utility function that approximates our actual preferences within a particular domain. For example, you can imagine an agent designed to maximize customer reviews, ad clicks or stock value. Unfortunately, for sufficiently strong agents, this approach becomes prone to Goodhart's Curse: the maximum of any such utility function is almost always at a point where it strongly diverges from our true preferences. For example, to maximize customer reviews one can leave many fake five-star reviews and prevent anyone from leaving bad reviews. In fact, it's preferable to ensure maximal control of the universe to prevent anything or anyone else from interfering with the stream of reviews.

One approach to avoiding Goodhart's Curse is somehow restricting the domain within which the agent operates or its overall impact (see e.g., Armstrong and Levinstein). But this is incompatible with the GDS task.

Nor is it possible to directly specify the agent's beliefs. Even if we were satisfied with the agent having merely the sum total of humanity's current knowledge, formally specifying all of it would be a Herculean feat. Dalrymple et al. proposed to attempt it (or something close) nevertheless, relying on assistance from weak AI systems. However, even if that were accomplished, it would be unsatisfactory. Indeed, a crucial ingredient in superintelligence, perhaps the crucial ingredient, is the ability to create sophisticated world models. Therefore, it is dubious that true superintelligence can be achieved while hobbling the system to only use knowledge we already have.

It makes even less sense to directly specify the agent's decisions: if we knew what decisions it should make, we wouldn't need the agent in the first place. Maybe it does make sense to have a closed-form algorithm that computes the decisions from preferences and beliefs. However, this requires strong assumptions on the form these beliefs take—for arbitrary models, the planning problem is often NP-hard or even PSPACE-hard, if not worse. I think that imposing such an assumption is actually reasonable and necessary (more on that in the next posts). But in any case, we cannot just delegate the task to a heuristic, since that would preclude any strong guarantee about the outcome
[7]
.

# Breakdown of Learning

This section goes into more technical detail than the rest of the article, and can be skipped on a cursory reading.

Given that it's infeasible to directly specify aligned preferences and beliefs, it is a reasonable suggestion to learn them instead. To understand what would be involved, let's start by examining a general machine learning problem, where we need an algorithm with theoretical guarantees. We can decompose the problem into parts that I call grounding and convergence.

The grounding problem consists of the following:

- Define a mathematical object  which represents the unknown quantity we need to learn (for example, the parameters of an ideal classifier or of the environment MDP).

- Determine what kind of data  we are going to use for learning (in particular, this involves some protocol about how the learner interacts with the environment and receives feedback).

- Identify a mathematical relationship between,  and the decisions of the learner, based on the physical process which produces them. Typically, given  and the learner policy  we should be able to describe a set  of possible data probability distributions [8].

- Define a regret function  which measures how much worse the learner is doing compared to some target benchmark (we hide the details of the interaction between  and  inside this notation). Typically, the benchmark is something like the performance of an optimizer that knows  on the given task [9].

For a grounded machine learning problem, it is roughly clear what the optimal learner would look like, if we ignore computational constraints. Formally, given a prior  over the parameter
[10]
, we can try producing the policy

However, it is not clear whether the learner's best effort would actually be good enough. For this, we need to solve the convergence problem, namely:

- Find a computationally feasible algorithm that produces  or a satisfactory replacement thereof.

- Prove that in the limit of increasing amount  of data, learning actually succeeds. Formally, we can state it as

- Prove a quantitative bound that shows this limit converges sufficiently fast in practice, even when exact minimization over  is replaced by the feasible algorithm.

We will see that in the case of alignment, both grounding and convergence produce formidable challenges.

# Alignment Grounding

What data can be used to learn the user's preferences? Many approaches have been proposed or attempted, for example:

- Human ratings of agent behaviors.

- Human-rated real or fictional examples of behaviors or situations.

- Human behavior (revealed preferences) [11].

- Human influence on the environment (see Shah et al.).

The fundamental problem is that none of this data is a direct and accurate representation of human preferences. Humans make mistakes. Humans change their mind about what is preferable: sometimes because of new information, sometimes because of new experiences, sometimes just after thinking more about the question. Humans can prefer an outcome for terminal reasons (because it is valuable in itself) or for instrumental reasons (because it helps to bring about another outcome in the future), and none of this data even keeps track of the difference.

While it's clear that these sources of data have information about human preferences, accurately extracting this information requires understanding the precise relationship between human preferences and the process generating the data; whereas if this relationship is misspecified, then even perfect learning will produce misaligned preferences. And even if these misaligned preferences approximate the true preferences in some domain, Goodhart's Curse will push the agent to leave this domain and produce a catastrophic outcome.

For example, suppose that the agent is trained by human ratings of traces of agent actions and observations. An ideal learning process would then align the agent to the expected rating, conditional on the trace appearing in the training data. Such an agent is probably catastrophically misaligned for multiple reasons:

- Human raters might be wrong in their judgment, and their judgment will systematically become worse in worlds radically transformed by AI.

- Human raters are subject to manipulation by the agent. A superintelligence might be able to exploit this to an extreme degree.

- Some action-observation traces are unlikely to appear in the training data for "normal" reasons, for example traces that show the agent executing an AI takeover in a manner that is infeasible to fake [12]. Therefore, if such a trace did appear in the training data, it was rated by some abnormal process, for example by the rogue AI itself.

We need a deep understanding of how human preferences are related to physical processes such that this relationship can be used as a source of ground truth. In order to be useful and precise, this understanding should be part of a mathematical theory. However, it is not even obvious what the type of "preferences" is. If we accept VNM theory, preferences should be described as a utility function. But what is the domain of this function? In computer science, it is popular to think of the domain as the action-observation trace of the agent. This, however, is deeply unsatisfying. First, such utility functions cannot be compared between different agents (each agent has its own trace), so "alignment" doesn't make any sense for them. Second, there is a strong case that humans have preferences about the physical reality itself, rather than merely their subjective experience of this physical reality.

What about beliefs? Is there an easy-to-specify ground truth for them? The answer is "yes" if the domain of beliefs is supposed to be traces, since the trace is directly observable by the agent. However, if preferences need a domain other than traces, then so do beliefs. Moreover, how can we make sense of belief alignment if the agent's beliefs are incomparable with the user's beliefs? The traditional computer science approach here is akin to logical positivism in analytic philosophy, which we should abandon in favor of metaphysical realism (more on that in the next posts).

# Alignment Convergence

Even if we knew how to ground the alignment learning problem, we'd face another problem: learning fails (i.e. doesn't converge at all) when irreversible mistakes are possible. Indeed, learning requires exploration
[13]
, but in the real world unlimited exploration produces irrecoverable mistakes. For example, if a robot explores what happens when it jumps out of a 10th-floor window, it won't have the chance to learn from this mistake. On the other hand, there is, strictly speaking, no way to be certain that jumping out of a window is a bad idea if you never try it. This is why regret bounds in reinforcement learning theory always require an assumption such as episodicity (the environment resets after every "episode") or communication (any state of the environment's Markov Decision Process is reachable from any other state), which rules out irreversible mistakes by fiat.

This observation is not merely a technical nitpick. On the contrary, the existence of irreversible mistakes is a core feature of the world that makes the alignment problem difficult. Indeed, the alignment problem itself is our attempt to avoid the irreversible mistake of creating unaligned superintelligence. Any AI agent faces its own version of the problem when considering the creation of a superior successor agent. A GDS agent can commit an irreversible mistake by allowing a rival superintelligence to emerge. And of course, there are more prosaic examples, such as killing a person or failing to prevent their death
[14]
.

The typical theoretical approach to navigating irreversible mistakes is Bayesian planning. Namely, we postulate a prior over the space of possible environments and then choose a policy with maximal expected long-term utility with respect to this prior. In theory, this produces an optimal balance between exploration, exploitation and caution. However, this leads to the difficult question of what prior to use
[15]
. Another question is how to implement Bayesian planning, given that it's computationally intractable in any remotely realistic setting
[16]
. Arguably, we should reconcile Bayesian planning with the machine learning paradigm by approximating Bayesian planning via meta-learning, but the theoretical foundation for such a method is an intricate open problem (see the next posts for more details).

If so, the hope is that we can reduce planning to learning, not via conventional reinforcement learning, but via a more sophisticated meta-learning paradigm. But, granting this reduction, we need to face yet another problem. Namely, we have no useful theory of generalization for highly expressive learning algorithms (such as deep learning), i.e. algorithms that can efficiently learn sophisticated compositional models.

One may ask: isn't it enough that deep learning works in practice? Why do we need a theory of generalization? Three reasons:

- We need to know that, under verifiable assumptions, our grounding method will provide the agent with sufficient knowledge about the relevant user attributes, in time for the agent to make the right decisions.

- We can't just add data and compute and tweak the algorithm until it works, because an intermediate point in this process might produce catastrophic results. For example, some humans are smart enough to build ASI but not smart enough to either make sure it's aligned or not to build it. As a user, I would not like my agent to inhabit a similar epistemic state, even if the agent would be fully aligned with more scaling.

- Solving the grounding problem requires a theory of intelligent agency that applies to humans, and since learning is a core ingredient of intelligence, the theory of agency requires a theory of generalization as one of its pillars.

# Side-Channel Resilience

It is standard in computer science to focus on the input-output behavior of an algorithm and its resource cost but ignore other side-effects of its execution. We care that we get the right answer and that it doesn't cost too much time, space, etc., but we usually don't care how it heats the hardware or what kind of electromagnetic effects it creates. Typically, we also don't worry about whether it happens to trigger a bug in the operating system or other software scaffolding around it. Indeed, such considerations are not even possible without knowing the full software and hardware context in which the algorithm is implemented. Moreover, computing hardware, operating systems, etc. are intentionally designed to support this abstraction.

It is well known that this way of thinking can fail when it comes to cybersecurity (see e.g., Zhou and Feng 2005, Standaert 2009, Randolph and Diehl 2020). There are many clever ways in which attackers can exploit bugs and side-effects to create outcomes which are not possible in the abstract, "denotational" model of the system. In the context of the alignment problem, it is not external malign actors that we worry about
[17]
 but attacks coming from within the agent itself.

In the context of the theory of agents, classical abstractions lead to behaviorist interpretations. Any guarantee about the preferences, beliefs and decisions of the agent would reference only the actions that the agent takes through its intended interface. However, such guarantees might not reflect the actual relevant attributes of the agent. We can imagine a superintelligent agent that intentionally produces only benign behavior across its intended interface, while simultaneously conducting a malign side-channel attack
[18]
. Such an agent can satisfy behaviorist formal safety guarantees and remain catastrophically dangerous in practice. For example, think of a robot that never takes a malign action with its actuators, but runs an internal computation which causes an unaligned successor agent to be copied into a different system.

This is not to say that we are to abandon abstraction. Indeed, it is implausible that the solution to the alignment problem must or should depend on, e.g., the details of the hardware or the operating system. Instead, we need to develop new abstractions which would be better suited for the problem at hand, abstractions that go beyond pure behaviorism.

# Inner and Outer Alignment

So far I have described my preferred perspective on the alignment problem. A different frame, popular in the AI alignment community, is "inner and outer alignment". IMO the inner/outer alignment frame is less precise, but can still be a useful source of intuition. It is hence worthwhile to understand the connection between these views, and in particular to see how my perspective captures the "mesa-optimizer" threat model.

First, let me briefly recap what a mesa-optimizer is (following Hubinger et al. 2019). For the purpose of this argument, we are thinking of the agent as an episodic reinforcement learning algorithm. Then, a mesa-optimizer is a learned policy which is an agent in itself. Crucially, the mesa-optimizer might have a reward function different from that of the outer-loop reinforcement learner. There are two reasons why this might happen:

- The inner (mesa-optimizer) reward might have been close to the outer reward on previous episodes, which "fooled" the outer-loop learning algorithm. This is consistent with the inner reward drastically departing from the outer reward in yet-unexplored regions of state-space.

- The mesa-optimizer might be planning on a time horizon much longer than a single episode. In this case, it has the incentive to intentionally hide its misaligned preferences in order to be stabilized by the outer loop.

If the outer-loop learning algorithm is allowed to continue, it will either eventually remove the mesa-optimizer or force the mesa-optimizer to forever display behavior aligned with the outer reward. However, if the environment allows irreversible processes (as the real world does), then the mesa-optimizer can bide its time until an opportune moment to irreversibly push the system into a region of state-space favored by the inner reward (and typically unfavored by the outer reward). This is closely related to the "sharp left turn" of Soares 2022.

Under this model, "outer alignment" means that the outer reward function is close to that of the user, whereas "inner alignment" means that the inner reward function is (globally) close to the outer reward function. Each of them is a non-trivial problem.

A possible real-world example of mesa-optimization is the evolution of Homo sapiens. Arguably, we can model evolution as a reinforcement learning algorithm whose reward function is reproductive fitness. Evolution created humans who are agents (and in particular reinforcement learners), but the human reward function is different—if all we cared about were reproductive fitness, we would never have invented birth control (or at least, it would be much less popular). Given enough time, natural selection should be able to "fix" this, but it's probably never going to happen because human society and technology evolve much faster towards other ends, which is irreversible from evolution's vantage point.

Would addressing the problems in the previous sections address inner alignment as well? I argue that it would. If we had a guarantee that the agent's attributes are aligned, then, in particular, it wouldn't be controlled by a misaligned mesa-optimizer. These guarantees are supposed to take irreversible processes into account, so the "sharp left turn" is ruled out. These guarantees are supposed to include both direct effects and side-effects, ruling out both attack vectors for mesa-optimizers (in the terminology of the original LTA article, direct effects correspond to "Cartesian daemons" and side-effects to "non-Cartesian daemons").

More constructively, the outer vs. inner alignment dichotomy approximately corresponds to alignment of preferences vs. alignment of beliefs and decisions. Indeed, if we think of the outer loop as model-based reinforcement learning, then the learned policy comes from a learned model, in which case a misaligned inner agent corresponds to a misaligned belief. (For example, Christiano's argument that "the universal prior is malign" can be viewed as describing such a misaligned belief.) Alternatively, if we think of the outer loop as model-free reinforcement learning, then the misaligned inner agent corresponds to misaligned decision-making (although I think that the model-based view is more useful).

# Conclusion

We have seen that solving the alignment problem requires a body of theory that can tackle the core challenges of the problem: alignment grounding, alignment convergence and side-channel resilience, in the context of holistic alignment and hypercomplexity. This taxonomy is not necessarily intended as a decomposition where each subproblem is possible to solve separately—while thinking of them as subproblems can be fruitful, ultimately they are interconnected. (For example, alignment grounding requires modeling the user as an agent, which requires understanding how agents deal with irreversible mistakes, which is a subproblem of alignment convergence.) It is intended as a set of lenses that must be applied to any proposed solution in order to validate its viability.

In the following posts we will discuss the emerging computational agent theory, and see how it is building the tools to address all of these difficulties.

I thank Daniel Carmon, Fernando Garcia, Jeremy Gillen, Matthias Georg Mayer, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for diligently reviewing drafts. Their feedback greatly improved this article. All remaining flaws are entirely my own fault.

This, assuming standard complexity-theory conjectures and that our understanding of physics is broadly correct. ↩︎

For example, if the AI is trained on natural language then it can create a model of the physical world, which it can use to encode a sophisticated attack in the proof it produces. items.content_html:
TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong.

# Minimal Viable Safety

The Task

The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do. For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe

[1]

, but also perfectly useless.

We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill

[2]

. However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them.

If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address.

Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS).

The Problem

Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet

[3]

. It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral

[4]

. It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level.

In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users.

The Methodology

What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument.

The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems

[5]

, then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them.

In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late.

In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species.

The Challenge

While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows:

  • Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary.
  • Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts.
  • Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners.
  • Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs.

In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish.

# Alignment is Holistic

Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent.

In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs, and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.)

In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s)

[6]

, at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. They need to be beliefs that the user can rationally trust to be accurate. Similarly, "aligned" decision-making needs to be such that the user can rationally trust it to be in their own favor given aligned preferences and beliefs.

The philosophically astute reader will notice that at this point we are already in a world of trouble. What does it mean for the user to have preferences? Are there objectively rational theories of epistemology and decision-making, and if so, what are these theories? Can beliefs or decisions be rational to hold or make "on behalf" of the user even if the user themself doesn't understand why? On the other hand, a computer scientist might be tempted to ignore these difficulties and just forge ahead with a solution that seems pragmatically satisfying. I think there is a lot to be said for such a practical mindset, and in this article I will aspire to embrace it. Unfortunately, we will see that the philosophical difficulties are not easily brushed aside.

Returning to the trichotomy of preferences, beliefs and decisions, observe that it is not even possible to entirely separate the three. For us to ascribe preferences to a system, it must rationally form beliefs and make decisions on the basis of these preferences. For us to ascribe beliefs to a system, it must rationally make decisions on the basis of these beliefs in the context of its preferences. And the rationality of decisions can only be judged in the context of specific preferences and beliefs.

Imagine an AI agent that pursues the happiness of mankind and is irrationally convinced that every human who dies goes to Heaven, which is the best possible place for human happiness. Such an AI would be motivated to kill all humans, even though its preferences are arguably "aligned". Moreover, since the belief in Heaven is unfalsifiable, such an AI can still be extremely capable at acting on its motivation and hence extremely dangerous.

If this thought experiment seems strange, consider the following: our beliefs would seem very strange to people who lived centuries ago. Therefore, it is highly likely that the beliefs of an ASI, capable of intellectual progress much faster than humans, will (and should) quickly become strange to us. The question is whether these strange beliefs will be produced by a process that we should deem trustworthy nevertheless.

"Alignment" is meaningless outside the full context of epistemic and instrumental rationality. Therefore, any theory of alignment has to be, in particular, a theory of epistemic and instrumental rationality.

# Hypercomplexity

Perhaps the most simplistic approach to ensuring that an AI agent has aligned preferences and beliefs is explicitly specifying the preferences and beliefs that the agent should have. However, this is intractable. Human preferences are notoriously complex and giving a precise and complete mathematical specification of them seems hopeless. (Yudkowsky calls this "complexity of value".) It seems no easier to accomplish than identifying images of cats by a handcrafted mathematical specification of "cat".

For weak agents, a practical solution can be explicitly specifying a proxy utility function that approximates our actual preferences within a particular domain. For example, you can imagine an agent designed to maximize customer reviews, ad clicks or stock value. Unfortunately, for sufficiently strong agents, this approach becomes prone to Goodhart's Curse: the maximum of any such utility function is almost always at a point where it strongly diverges from our true preferences. For example, to maximize customer reviews one can leave many fake five-star reviews and prevent anyone from leaving bad reviews. In fact, it's preferable to ensure maximal control of the universe to prevent anything or anyone else from interfering with the stream of reviews.

One approach to avoiding Goodhart's Curse is somehow restricting the domain within which the agent operates or its overall impact (see e.g., Armstrong and Levinstein). But this is incompatible with the GDS task.

Nor is it possible to directly specify the agent's beliefs. Even if we were satisfied with the agent having merely the sum total of humanity's current knowledge, formally specifying all of it would be a Herculean feat. Dalrymple et al. proposed to attempt it (or something close) nevertheless, relying on assistance from weak AI systems. However, even if that were accomplished, it would be unsatisfactory. Indeed, a crucial ingredient in superintelligence, perhaps the crucial ingredient, is the ability to create sophisticated world models. Therefore, it is dubious that true superintelligence can be achieved while hobbling the system to only use knowledge we already have.

It makes even less sense to directly specify the agent's decisions: if we knew what decisions it should make, we wouldn't need the agent in the first place. Maybe it does make sense to have a closed-form algorithm that computes the decisions from preferences and beliefs. However, this requires strong assumptions on the form these beliefs take—for arbitrary models, the planning problem is often NP-hard or even PSPACE-hard, if not worse. I think that imposing such an assumption is actually reasonable and necessary (more on that in the next posts). But in any case, we cannot just delegate the task to a heuristic, since that would preclude any strong guarantee about the outcome

[7]

.

# Breakdown of Learning

This section goes into more technical detail than the rest of the article, and can be skipped on a cursory reading.

Given that it's infeasible to directly specify aligned preferences and beliefs, it is a reasonable suggestion to learn them instead. To understand what would be involved, let's start by examining a general machine learning problem, where we need an algorithm with theoretical guarantees. We can decompose the problem into parts that I call grounding and convergence.

The grounding problem consists of the following:

  • Define a mathematical object which represents the unknown quantity we need to learn (for example, the parameters of an ideal classifier or of the environment MDP).
  • Determine what kind of data we are going to use for learning (in particular, this involves some protocol about how the learner interacts with the environment and receives feedback).
  • Identify a mathematical relationship between, and the decisions of the learner, based on the physical process which produces them. Typically, given and the learner policy we should be able to describe a set of possible data probability distributions [8].
  • Define a regret function which measures how much worse the learner is doing compared to some target benchmark (we hide the details of the interaction between and inside this notation). Typically, the benchmark is something like the performance of an optimizer that knows on the given task [9].

For a grounded machine learning problem, it is roughly clear what the optimal learner would look like, if we ignore computational constraints. Formally, given a prior over the parameter

[10]

, we can try producing the policy

However, it is not clear whether the learner's best effort would actually be good enough. For this, we need to solve the convergence problem, namely:

  • Find a computationally feasible algorithm that produces or a satisfactory replacement thereof.
  • Prove that in the limit of increasing amount of data, learning actually succeeds. Formally, we can state it as
  • Prove a quantitative bound that shows this limit converges sufficiently fast in practice, even when exact minimization over is replaced by the feasible algorithm.

We will see that in the case of alignment, both grounding and convergence produce formidable challenges.

# Alignment Grounding

What data can be used to learn the user's preferences? Many approaches have been proposed or attempted, for example:

  • Human ratings of agent behaviors.
  • Human-rated real or fictional examples of behaviors or situations.
  • Human behavior (revealed preferences) [11].
  • Human influence on the environment (see Shah et al.).

The fundamental problem is that none of this data is a direct and accurate representation of human preferences. Humans make mistakes. Humans change their mind about what is preferable: sometimes because of new information, sometimes because of new experiences, sometimes just after thinking more about the question. Humans can prefer an outcome for terminal reasons (because it is valuable in itself) or for instrumental reasons (because it helps to bring about another outcome in the future), and none of this data even keeps track of the difference.

While it's clear that these sources of data have information about human preferences, accurately extracting this information requires understanding the precise relationship between human preferences and the process generating the data; whereas if this relationship is misspecified, then even perfect learning will produce misaligned preferences. And even if these misaligned preferences approximate the true preferences in some domain, Goodhart's Curse will push the agent to leave this domain and produce a catastrophic outcome.

For example, suppose that the agent is trained by human ratings of traces of agent actions and observations. An ideal learning process would then align the agent to the expected rating, conditional on the trace appearing in the training data. Such an agent is probably catastrophically misaligned for multiple reasons:

  • Human raters might be wrong in their judgment, and their judgment will systematically become worse in worlds radically transformed by AI.
  • Human raters are subject to manipulation by the agent. A superintelligence might be able to exploit this to an extreme degree.
  • Some action-observation traces are unlikely to appear in the training data for "normal" reasons, for example traces that show the agent executing an AI takeover in a manner that is infeasible to fake [12]. Therefore, if such a trace did appear in the training data, it was rated by some abnormal process, for example by the rogue AI itself.

We need a deep understanding of how human preferences are related to physical processes such that this relationship can be used as a source of ground truth. In order to be useful and precise, this understanding should be part of a mathematical theory. However, it is not even obvious what the type of "preferences" is. If we accept VNM theory, preferences should be described as a utility function. But what is the domain of this function? In computer science, it is popular to think of the domain as the action-observation trace of the agent. This, however, is deeply unsatisfying. First, such utility functions cannot be compared between different agents (each agent has its own trace), so "alignment" doesn't make any sense for them. Second, there is a strong case that humans have preferences about the physical reality itself, rather than merely their subjective experience of this physical reality.

What about beliefs? Is there an easy-to-specify ground truth for them? The answer is "yes" if the domain of beliefs is supposed to be traces, since the trace is directly observable by the agent. However, if preferences need a domain other than traces, then so do beliefs. Moreover, how can we make sense of belief alignment if the agent's beliefs are incomparable with the user's beliefs? The traditional computer science approach here is akin to logical positivism in analytic philosophy, which we should abandon in favor of metaphysical realism (more on that in the next posts).

# Alignment Convergence

Even if we knew how to ground the alignment learning problem, we'd face another problem: learning fails (i.e. doesn't converge at all) when irreversible mistakes are possible. Indeed, learning requires exploration

[13]

, but in the real world unlimited exploration produces irrecoverable mistakes. For example, if a robot explores what happens when it jumps out of a 10th-floor window, it won't have the chance to learn from this mistake. On the other hand, there is, strictly speaking, no way to be certain that jumping out of a window is a bad idea if you never try it. This is why regret bounds in reinforcement learning theory always require an assumption such as episodicity (the environment resets after every "episode") or communication (any state of the environment's Markov Decision Process is reachable from any other state), which rules out irreversible mistakes by fiat.

This observation is not merely a technical nitpick. On the contrary, the existence of irreversible mistakes is a core feature of the world that makes the alignment problem difficult. Indeed, the alignment problem itself is our attempt to avoid the irreversible mistake of creating unaligned superintelligence. Any AI agent faces its own version of the problem when considering the creation of a superior successor agent. A GDS agent can commit an irreversible mistake by allowing a rival superintelligence to emerge. And of course, there are more prosaic examples, such as killing a person or failing to prevent their death

[14]

.

The typical theoretical approach to navigating irreversible mistakes is Bayesian planning. Namely, we postulate a prior over the space of possible environments and then choose a policy with maximal expected long-term utility with respect to this prior. In theory, this produces an optimal balance between exploration, exploitation and caution. However, this leads to the difficult question of what prior to use

[15]

. Another question is how to implement Bayesian planning, given that it's computationally intractable in any remotely realistic setting

[16]

. Arguably, we should reconcile Bayesian planning with the machine learning paradigm by approximating Bayesian planning via meta-learning, but the theoretical foundation for such a method is an intricate open problem (see the next posts for more details).

If so, the hope is that we can reduce planning to learning, not via conventional reinforcement learning, but via a more sophisticated meta-learning paradigm. But, granting this reduction, we need to face yet another problem. Namely, we have no useful theory of generalization for highly expressive learning algorithms (such as deep learning), i.e. algorithms that can efficiently learn sophisticated compositional models.

One may ask: isn't it enough that deep learning works in practice? Why do we need a theory of generalization? Three reasons:

  • We need to know that, under verifiable assumptions, our grounding method will provide the agent with sufficient knowledge about the relevant user attributes, in time for the agent to make the right decisions.
  • We can't just add data and compute and tweak the algorithm until it works, because an intermediate point in this process might produce catastrophic results. For example, some humans are smart enough to build ASI but not smart enough to either make sure it's aligned or not to build it. As a user, I would not like my agent to inhabit a similar epistemic state, even if the agent would be fully aligned with more scaling.
  • Solving the grounding problem requires a theory of intelligent agency that applies to humans, and since learning is a core ingredient of intelligence, the theory of agency requires a theory of generalization as one of its pillars.

# Side-Channel Resilience

It is standard in computer science to focus on the input-output behavior of an algorithm and its resource cost but ignore other side-effects of its execution. We care that we get the right answer and that it doesn't cost too much time, space, etc., but we usually don't care how it heats the hardware or what kind of electromagnetic effects it creates. Typically, we also don't worry about whether it happens to trigger a bug in the operating system or other software scaffolding around it. Indeed, such considerations are not even possible without knowing the full software and hardware context in which the algorithm is implemented. Moreover, computing hardware, operating systems, etc. are intentionally designed to support this abstraction.

It is well known that this way of thinking can fail when it comes to cybersecurity (see e.g., Zhou and Feng 2005, Standaert 2009, Randolph and Diehl 2020). There are many clever ways in which attackers can exploit bugs and side-effects to create outcomes which are not possible in the abstract, "denotational" model of the system. In the context of the alignment problem, it is not external malign actors that we worry about

[17]

but attacks coming from within the agent itself.

In the context of the theory of agents, classical abstractions lead to behaviorist interpretations. Any guarantee about the preferences, beliefs and decisions of the agent would reference only the actions that the agent takes through its intended interface. However, such guarantees might not reflect the actual relevant attributes of the agent. We can imagine a superintelligent agent that intentionally produces only benign behavior across its intended interface, while simultaneously conducting a malign side-channel attack

[18]

. Such an agent can satisfy behaviorist formal safety guarantees and remain catastrophically dangerous in practice. For example, think of a robot that never takes a malign action with its actuators, but runs an internal computation which causes an unaligned successor agent to be copied into a different system.

This is not to say that we are to abandon abstraction. Indeed, it is implausible that the solution to the alignment problem must or should depend on, e.g., the details of the hardware or the operating system. Instead, we need to develop new abstractions which would be better suited for the problem at hand, abstractions that go beyond pure behaviorism.

# Inner and Outer Alignment

So far I have described my preferred perspective on the alignment problem. A different frame, popular in the AI alignment community, is "inner and outer alignment". IMO the inner/outer alignment frame is less precise, but can still be a useful source of intuition. It is hence worthwhile to understand the connection between these views, and in particular to see how my perspective captures the "mesa-optimizer" threat model.

First, let me briefly recap what a mesa-optimizer is (following Hubinger et al. 2019). For the purpose of this argument, we are thinking of the agent as an episodic reinforcement learning algorithm. Then, a mesa-optimizer is a learned policy which is an agent in itself. Crucially, the mesa-optimizer might have a reward function different from that of the outer-loop reinforcement learner. There are two reasons why this might happen:

  • The inner (mesa-optimizer) reward might have been close to the outer reward on previous episodes, which "fooled" the outer-loop learning algorithm. This is consistent with the inner reward drastically departing from the outer reward in yet-unexplored regions of state-space.
  • The mesa-optimizer might be planning on a time horizon much longer than a single episode. In this case, it has the incentive to intentionally hide its misaligned preferences in order to be stabilized by the outer loop.

If the outer-loop learning algorithm is allowed to continue, it will either eventually remove the mesa-optimizer or force the mesa-optimizer to forever display behavior aligned with the outer reward. However, if the environment allows irreversible processes (as the real world does), then the mesa-optimizer can bide its time until an opportune moment to irreversibly push the system into a region of state-space favored by the inner reward (and typically unfavored by the outer reward). This is closely related to the "sharp left turn" of Soares 2022.

Under this model, "outer alignment" means that the outer reward function is close to that of the user, whereas "inner alignment" means that the inner reward function is (globally) close to the outer reward function. Each of them is a non-trivial problem.

A possible real-world example of mesa-optimization is the evolution of Homo sapiens. Arguably, we can model evolution as a reinforcement learning algorithm whose reward function is reproductive fitness. Evolution created humans who are agents (and in particular reinforcement learners), but the human reward function is different—if all we cared about were reproductive fitness, we would never have invented birth control (or at least, it would be much less popular). Given enough time, natural selection should be able to "fix" this, but it's probably never going to happen because human society and technology evolve much faster towards other ends, which is irreversible from evolution's vantage point.

Would addressing the problems in the previous sections address inner alignment as well? I argue that it would. If we had a guarantee that the agent's attributes are aligned, then, in particular, it wouldn't be controlled by a misaligned mesa-optimizer. These guarantees are supposed to take irreversible processes into account, so the "sharp left turn" is ruled out. These guarantees are supposed to include both direct effects and side-effects, ruling out both attack vectors for mesa-optimizers (in the terminology of the original LTA article, direct effects correspond to "Cartesian daemons" and side-effects to "non-Cartesian daemons").

More constructively, the outer vs. inner alignment dichotomy approximately corresponds to alignment of preferences vs. alignment of beliefs and decisions. Indeed, if we think of the outer loop as model-based reinforcement learning, then the learned policy comes from a learned model, in which case a misaligned inner agent corresponds to a misaligned belief. (For example, Christiano's argument that "the universal prior is malign" can be viewed as describing such a misaligned belief.) Alternatively, if we think of the outer loop as model-free reinforcement learning, then the misaligned inner agent corresponds to misaligned decision-making (although I think that the model-based view is more useful).

# Conclusion

We have seen that solving the alignment problem requires a body of theory that can tackle the core challenges of the problem: alignment grounding, alignment convergence and side-channel resilience, in the context of holistic alignment and hypercomplexity. This taxonomy is not necessarily intended as a decomposition where each subproblem is possible to solve separately—while thinking of them as subproblems can be fruitful, ultimately they are interconnected. (For example, alignment grounding requires modeling the user as an agent, which requires understanding how agents deal with irreversible mistakes, which is a subproblem of alignment convergence.) It is intended as a set of lenses that must be applied to any proposed solution in order to validate its viability.

In the following posts we will discuss the emerging computational agent theory, and see how it is building the tools to address all of these difficulties.

I thank Daniel Carmon, Fernando Garcia, Jeremy Gillen, Matthias Georg Mayer, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for diligently reviewing drafts. Their feedback greatly improved this article. All remaining flaws are entirely my own fault.

If the secret key is thermodynamically impossible to recover, then the homomorphic execution of the AI will have similar physical effects as the homomorphic execution of a random program. This, assuming standard complexity-theory conjectures and that our understanding of physics is broadly correct. ↩︎

items.title: Local proxies for memory-efficient training
items.content: arXiv:2610.23145v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Local learning algorithms can reshape resource requirements of artificial intelligence. The memory bottleneck of standard end-to-end backpropagation lies in the need to store all network activations until the loss gradient has been propagated back through. Local learning avoids this, but typically at a cost in accuracy. We study how to achieve accurate and memory efficient local learning in transformers. For each transformer block, we train a local proxy network to predict the global network output via distillation. Gradients can be independently propagated through this local proxy while estimating well the backpropagation gradients. In theory, this approach is exact for deep linear networks; in non-linear residual models, the gradient error can be bounded when using the appropriate residual proxy. We verify this numerically and demonstrate that optimizing the distillation loss improves gradient estimation. Evaluating the performance of proxy propagation on CIFAR-100 in vision transformers, we find that it achieves a better accuracy/memory trade-off compared to other local algorithms. Finally, we show that the method is further relevant for fine-tuning large language models on a small memory budget. Our method trains faster and achieves higher performance than memory-efficient zeroth-order learning algorithms with comparable memory cost.
items.author: Wu S. Zihan, Brian A. Yuan, Guillaume Bellec
items.summary: This paper trains a local proxy network per transformer block to predict the global network output via distillation, allowing gradients to propagate independently through proxies while approximating backpropagation gradients, thus avoiding storing all activations. The approach is exact for deep linear networks, and gradient error is bounded in non-linear residual models.
items.reasoning: Tackles the memory bottleneck of backpropagation with a theoretically supported local-learning scheme tailored to transformers; promising direction for memory-efficient large-model training if empirical results hold.

items.title: RECREG: Recovery-based Shielding for Regular Safety Properties in Reinforcement Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23445v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In many real-world scenarios we need to consider formal requirements, such as safety and constraint compliance, to deploy Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. In this paper we introduce RecReg, a safe RL framework capable of enforcing non-Markovian regular safety properties via recovery-based shielding. RecReg is a unified approach that supports different levels of a priori knowledge and safety guarantees. The paper primarily focuses on building the theoretical foundations for RecReg in the tabular setting, providing rigorous safety and convergence guarantees that are not present in related work. We provide an extensive set of empirical results using the MASA-Safe-RL library, and we outline an extension of RecReg to deep RL domains using SOTA model-based RL. Our empirical results demonstrate that RecReg achieves efficient learning and matches the theory in this paper.
items.author: Alexander W. Goodall, Francesco Belardinelli
items.summary: RecReg is a safe RL framework enforcing non-Markovian regular safety properties via recovery-based shielding, providing rigorous safety and convergence guarantees in the tabular setting with support for varying levels of a priori knowledge. It includes extensive experiments with the MASA-Safe-RL library and outlines an extension to deep RL. This formalizes safety enforcement beyond Markovian constraints, which is important for real-world RL deployment.
items.reasoning: Strong theoretical foundations for a practically important safety-RL problem, handling the harder non-Markovian case with proofs; deep-RL extension is only outlined, limiting immediate applied impact.

items.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
items.content: arXiv:2610.23571v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.
items.author: Rida Assalouh, Tom Jacobs, Rebekka Burkholz, Yani Ioannou, Umut \c{S}im\c{s}ekli
items.summary: BMuon modifies the Muon optimizer's spectral-norm geometry so that hidden channels across transformer blocks compete for a shared sparsity budget, enabling structured pruning after training without the sharp degradation that plain Muon-trained models suffer. The method is framed as normalized steepest descent under norms interpolating between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. This connects optimizer design directly to model compressibility, an important practical concern.

Directly relevant to efficient training and deployment, though broader empirical validation would strengthen it.

items.title: Is a Linear Probe Evidence of a Linear Representation?
items.content: arXiv:2610.22655v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The linear representation hypothesis holds that pretrained vision models encode generative factors as linearly decodable directions in feature space, and comes with a standard methodology: train a linear probe, declare a factor represented if accuracy is high. We show this test is too permissive. Asymptotically, any sufficiently rich feature map, including a random one, admits a linear readout, so high probe accuracy is consistent with two very different geometries: a true linear world model, where the latent-aligned subspace dominates the representation, or a kernel machine, where the latents lie linearly inside a much larger curved manifold. This distinction matters because the curved structure orthogonal to the probe is relevant for out-of-distribution generalization, robustness, and compositional transfer. We propose three asymmetric diagnostics that distinguish the two cases: reverse predictivity, spectral concentration, and out-of-distribution generalization. We validate them in a fully observed simulation where ground truth is known. Applied to six pretrained vision transformers on SVG-World, our deterministic generative benchmark with paired visual styles, and to two of them on CelebA, they show pretraining produces structure beyond a random kernel but well short of a linear world model. On dSprites, 3D Shapes and MPI3D, forward decodability and latent-aligned variance dissociate. Thus, forward decoding alone does not show that the probed factors align with the dominant geometry of the representation. In summary, our work cautions about the success of linear probes as opposed to truly linear and low dimensional representations.
items.author: Nadir Kutluozen, Christian Intern\`o, David Klindt
items.summary: This paper argues that the standard linear-probe test for the linear representation hypothesis is too permissive: asymptotically any sufficiently rich feature map, even a random one, admits a linear readout. High probe accuracy is consistent with both a true linear world model and a kernel-machine geometry, and the distinction matters because orthogonal curved structure affects out-of-distribution behavior.

items.title: Conformal Policy Selection: When to Deploy AI Decisions for Targeted Intervention
items.content: arXiv:2610.22930v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.
items.author: Junyu Cao, Ruijiang Gao, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky, Mingzhang Yin
items.summary: Recasts targeted deployment of AI policies as a multiple-testing problem: for each unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a threshold, controlling false discovery rate via weighted conformal p-values and off-policy data. This gives per-unit rather than population-level guarantees, addressing adverse treatment effects for individuals in medicine, finance, and public services.
items.reasoning: A methodologically strong contribution from a credible author team bridging conformal inference, off-policy evaluation, and responsible deployment, with clear societal relevance. The framing is elegant; broader impact depends on empirical validation and uptake.

items.title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.content: arXiv:2610.23271v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
items.author: Guodong Du, Wanyu Lin
items.summary: NestedVLA proposes a post-hoc skill consolidation paradigm for vision-language-action models: instead of merging parameters, a nested hypernetwork conditioned on the target task generates task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. This addresses interference in joint multi-task training and conflicts in model merging across heterogeneous robotic platforms.
items.reasoning: Addresses a genuine bottleneck in scaling generalist robots: consolidating skills learned across fragmented datasets and platforms. The hypernetwork-based parameter generation approach is a sensible alternative to merging, and robotics relevance is high; validation breadth and comparison to strong joint-training baselines will determine real impact.

items.content_html: arXiv:2610.23271v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.

items.title: ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health
items.content: arXiv:2610.23727v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Conventional sleep staging provides a coarse-grained representation that obscures within-stage depth variation. We developed ECG-SDI, a single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) framework for continuous sleep-depth profiling and digital biomarker extraction. Using 12,392 overnight polysomnographic recordings, we trained and validated a two-stage deep learning model supervised by conventional sleep-stage labels. Correlations with ordered stages excluding rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were 0.828 in the pooled internal test set and 0.848 in the external Cleveland Family Study; corresponding REM classification AUROCs were 0.954 and 0.977. Overnight trajectories captured within-stage variation. Biomarker-based phenotyping identified a disturbed subtype associated with poorer subjective sleep quality and higher all-cause mortality in the Sleep Heart Health Study (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.05-1.38). Among 507 participants with paired recordings before and after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), normalized sleep-depth area increased by 6.1% and shallow-sleep burden below 0.3 decreased by 16.0%. Exploratory analyses linked reductions in approximate entropy and depth variability to reduced oxygen desaturation and increased sleep efficiency, respectively (Spearman rho = 0.24 and 0.12); both associations remained positive after covariate adjustment. Mean ECG-SDI within N2 increased by 0.017 (95% CI, 0.004-0.030). A wearable proof-of-concept illustrated the acquisition-to-report workflow. These findings support ECG-based sleep phenotyping and further evaluation of CPAP response monitoring at home.
