items.title: JAXtari: High-Throughput and Easy-to-Modify Arcade Learning Environment
items.content: arXiv:2610.23650v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The Arcade Learning Environment (ALE) has been a cornerstone of Deep Reinforcement Learning research, providing a standardized benchmark for evaluating general agents. However, its lack of native support for object-extraction and environment modification restricts research into evaluating whether agents learn robust causal models or rely on brittle visual heuristics. Furthermore, the ALE's dependence on CPU-based emulation creates a significant bottleneck in modern GPU-accelerated training pipelines, limiting both experimental scale and iteration frequency. In this work, we introduce JAXtari, an open-source, high-performance reimplementation of Atari 2600 environments. By leveraging massive GPU parallelization, JAXtari allows PPO agents to finish training on 100M environment steps on a single A100-GPU in under an hour. Beyond speed, it provides object-centric observations and a flexible modification system, allowing researchers to, e.g. develop neuro-symbolic methods or discover novel shortcuts and subsequently train and adapt their agents rapidly, sometimes in only minutes.
items.author: Quentin Delfosse, Raban Emunds, Paul Seitz, Sebastian Wette, Jannis Bl\"uml, Daniel Kirn, Dominik Mandok, Kristian Kersting
items.summary: JAXtari is an open-source, GPU-parallelized reimplementation of the Arcade Learning Environment (Atari 2600) in JAX, addressing the CPU emulation bottleneck in modern RL pipelines. It natively supports object extraction and environment modification, enabling studies of whether agents learn causal models or brittle visual heuristics. PPO agents can reportedly train at substantially higher throughput than with the original ALE.
items.reasoning: A valuable infrastructure contribution following the successful JAX-based environment trend (e.g., in the lineage of GPU-accelerated emulators). High-throughput, modifiable Atari environments will likely see real adoption in RL research, though it is a reimplementation rather than a new method.

items.title: Where's the Indirect Evidence? Investigating Grammatical Generalization with Influence Functions
items.content: arXiv:2610.22919v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Language models generalize beyond their training corpus to learn linguistic phenomena (Patil et al., 2024; Misra and Mahowald, 2024), showing that there exists indirect evidence driving learning. Prior work has inferred that indirect evidence exists without identifying its character or considered specific hypotheses about what it might be. We explore an alternative bottom-up method for identifying indirect evidence. We use influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017) to measure how individual training sentences affect model predictions in 15 grammatical phenomena from BLiMP (Warstadt et al., 2020). We filter out a phenomenon's direct evidence using hand-constructed rules and take the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. This indirect evidence substantially affects learning: retraining without it lowers held-out accuracy more than removing a matched random group for every phenomenon across five models (by a median of 12 points). We characterize the indirect evidence by its similarity to our direct evidence filters: it (partially) meets the filters' structural conditions at a median of 4.7 times the rate of a matched random group. Finally, clustering phenomena by indirect-evidence overlap recovers three of the five BLiMP categories that include multiple phenomena, suggesting that this method can reveal linguistic relationships.
items.author: William Dai, Zhenghao Herbert Zhou, Maya Viswanathan, Robert Frank
items.summary: Uses influence functions to identify, bottom-up, which training sentences drive grammatical generalization across 15 BLiMP phenomena, filtering out direct evidence with hand-built rules and ranking the 60,000 most influential remaining sentences as indirect evidence. This goes beyond prior work that merely inferred indirect evidence exists or tested specific hypotheses about its nature.
items.reasoning: A strong linguistics-meets-interpretability study: applying influence functions at this scale to characterize what indirect evidence actually looks like advances understanding of how LMs generalize grammatically. Scoped to grammatical phenomena and smaller models typical of such analyses.

items.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.23372v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
items.author: Keyuan Luo, Yi Xie, Wanyun Ling, Yuanzhe Li, Ziyue Li, Zhuoqi Zeng

items.reasoning: A thoughtful evaluation-protocol contribution for an increasingly important question as memory-augmented agents proliferate: does memory causally help, and under what conditions? The interventional design is principled and transferable to LLM agents more broadly, though empirical scope is specific to VLA systems.

items.title: ConvexLLM: Scaling Convex-Hull Speech Interfaces to General-Purpose Audio Intelligence
items.content: arXiv:2610.23539v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Speech and audio language models connect continuous acoustic representations to decoders pretrained primarily on text data. Most such models use MLP or Q-Former interfaces to map acoustic features into the decoder's input space, requiring the decoder to learn how to interpret the resulting representations. We investigate whether grounding these representations in the decoder's existing text embeddings can help it use acoustic information while better preserving its pretrained text capabilities. We present ConvexLLM, a general-purpose speech and audio language model whose C-Gate interface represents audio as continuous convex combinations of frozen text embeddings. ConvexLLM achieves an eleven-task VoiceBench aggregate of 75.36, the highest among the open-weight models we compare, and an MMAU Test-mini accuracy of 62.50%. Its largest margins over the baselines are on spoken knowledge and reasoning tasks, while the strongest baselines are more accurate on audio understanding and transcription. In a comparison with a 2B-parameter decoder, C-Gate achieves higher aggregate spoken-language performance than MLP and Q-Former interfaces, with text-task performance close to MLP and task-dependent tradeoffs in transcription and audio understanding. These results support convex combinations of text embeddings as a viable interface for general-purpose speech and audio language models.

items.title: Are Large Reasoning Models Good Everyday Reasoners? A Comparison with Non-Reasoning Models on Logical Reasoning Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2610.22538v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) that leverage test-time computation achieve strong performance on mathematical and scientific benchmarks and are increasingly deployed in real-world applications. However, their ability to perform \textit{everyday logical reasoning}, which often departs from textbook formal logic, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate how well reasoning models align with everyday reasoning patterns by introducing a benchmark based on linguistic and pragmatic reasoning phenomena. We also compare reasoning models with non-reasoning models under controlled prompting conditions. We find that, in many cases, (1) reasoning models show degraded performance in everyday reasoning when such reasoning deviates from formal logical rules, (2) some non-reasoning models with chain-of-thought prompting outperform comparable reasoning models in everyday reasoning, and (3) prompting with additional instructions provides limited control over reasoning behavior. These findings suggest that current reasoning models do not reliably capture everyday reasoning and point to limitations in post-training, motivating improved training objectives and evaluation across diverse forms of reasoning.

items.reasoning: Provides a useful counterpoint to benchmark-driven enthusiasm for reasoning models, highlighting systematic weaknesses in pragmatic reasoning; solid evaluation work, though without new methods and with dependence on current model versions.

items.title: Too Emotional to Be Fake? Intra-Utterance Emotion Shifts Expose Failure Modes in Speech Deepfake Detectors
items.content: arXiv:2610.22832v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Expressive speech synthesis can now change emotion within a single utterance, yet its impact on deepfake detection remains unclear. We introduce EmoShift, a benchmark comparing emotion-stable (AA) and emotion-changing (AB) speech to examine these effects while accounting for static emotion identity and acoustic confounds. It comprises 7,240 bona fide utterances from four source datasets and 9,720 synthetic utterances generated using four expressive TTS systems. Across seven detectors, we find that emotion changes can make synthetic speech appear more genuine, increasing spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points on OMG-Emotion at fixed thresholds. Conversely, emotion-changing bona fide speech increases false-alarm rates by up to 24.4 percentage points on IEMOCAP. Further analyses reveal detector-specific sensitivities to emotion trajectories, not fully explained by static emotion identity or splicing artifacts. These findings underscore the importance of emotion dynamics in deepfake detection.
items.author: Jingyi Chen, Surya Koppisetti
items.summary: The paper introduces EmoShift, a benchmark with 7,240 bona fide and 9,720 synthetic utterances from four expressive TTS systems, comparing emotion-stable and emotion-changing speech to probe speech deepfake detectors. It finds intra-utterance emotion shifts make synthetic speech appear more genuine (raising spoof miss rates by up to 25.3 percentage points) and emotion-changing real speech raises false alarms by up to 24.4 points.
items.reasoning: Reveals a concrete, quantified vulnerability in deployed-class deepfake detectors using a well-controlled benchmark with acoustic confounds accounted for; security-relevant and timely as expressive TTS advances, though focused on detection rather than defense.

items.title: JAVIS: Joint Audio-Visual Interaction and Streaming for Real-Time Conversational Agents
items.content: arXiv:2610.22499v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Human communication is inherently multimodal, conveying intent not only through linguistic and vocal cues but also through visual signals. However, existing conversational systems have mainly focused on text or speech, leaving out the visual feedback that is essential for natural interaction. In this paper, we propose JAVIS, an end-to-end streaming framework for real-time audio-visual conversational agents. Our key idea is to let the voice and the face speak from a single representation. On top of a shared LLM, a Joint Refined Head produces a unified audio-visual representation, which is fed into dedicated streaming branches for speech and face generation. This end-to-end design avoids intermediate bottlenecks, enabling real-time generation while keeping speech and face tightly synchronized. In addition, we present JAVIS-Syn, a 334-hour synthetic corpus designed to address the lack of expressive audio-visual dialogue data, covering emotionally rich multi-turn conversations and assistant-style exchanges. Experiments show that JAVIS achieves approximately 200$\times$ lower initial latency than a strong baseline, while outperforming baselines in lip synchronization and facial expression appropriateness.
items.author: Junseok Ahn, Jaehyun Park, Jeongsoo Choi, Joon Son Chung, Ji-Hoon Kim
items.summary: JAVIS is an end-to-end streaming framework for real-time audio-visual conversational agents in which voice and face generation derive from a single shared representation produced by a Joint Refined Head atop a shared LLM. Dedicated streaming branches for speech and face generation avoid intermediate bottlenecks, enabling real-time multimodal generation. This extends conversational systems beyond text and speech to include visual feedback.
items.reasoning: Full-duplex audio-visual conversational agents are an active frontier, and the single-representation joint generation design is a coherent architectural contribution. Real-time constraints add engineering difficulty; the abstract suggests a strong system, but wider adoption and comparison to speech-only baselines will determine impact.

items.title: Three LiDARs, Twenty-Five Datasets: Cross-Source Generalization in Tree-Species Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2610.22606v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: FOR-species20K is the largest public LiDAR benchmark for tree-species classification, pooling 25 independently collected terrestrial, mobile, and airborne laser-scanning datasets across 33 species. We introduce a multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves official hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at the time of submission. We then examine what this score measures. Because the hidden test is species-balanced, its overall accuracy is more comparable to a macro metric than to accuracy under the public set's long-tailed distribution. Moreover, the official random split places every source dataset in both training and evaluation. A logistic probe recovers source identity from out-of-fold model probabilities with 69% accuracy, while geometric features identify the source above 90% within two widely shared species; 18 of the 33 species occur in only one source. Under a source-species-cell holdout, evaluated on 5,566 trees from eight eligible species that retain the same LiDAR-type training support in other sources, the unweighted species mean falls from 82% to 36%, and tree-weighted accuracy falls from 95% to 60%. Count-matched retraining and experiments with two alternative backbones indicate that this gap is not explained by reduced training support alone, while an external PureForest experiment shows a smaller but consistent grouped-split effect. These results establish the 85% leaderboard score as strong in-distribution performance, but not as an estimate of source-disjoint generalization, motivating balanced metrics and source-aware evaluation. The code is available at: https://github.com/JaeLee18/FOR20K-lidar-tree-species
items.author: Jae Joong Lee, Bedrich Benes
items.summary: The authors build a multi-resolution, multi-view ConvNeXtV2 model that improves the FOR-species20K LiDAR tree-species classification hidden-test accuracy from 79.5% to 85.0%, ranking first at submission. They then critically examine what the score measures, showing the species-balanced hidden test masks long-tailed behavior and that the official random split leaks source identity — a logistic probe recovers source from out-of-fold model probabilities. This exposes dataset-leakage issues in the benchmark.
items.reasoning: Combines a SOTA result with a genuinely important benchmark critique demonstrating source leakage, which has implications beyond forestry for any pooled multi-source dataset. The methodological audit is the most valuable part; domain reach is specialized but the lesson generalizes.

items.title: STRIDE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning in Driving Edge Cases
items.content: arXiv:2610.22795v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In autonomous driving, perceiving surrounding objects is not enough: failing to understand how they move and interact over time can lead to dangerous decisions. Evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) therefore requires testing whether they connect past spatial observations to future consequences. Yet existing benchmarks often assess edge cases through basic perception questions or test temporal understanding in simple scenarios, leaving complex spatiotemporal reasoning underexplored. We introduce STRIDE (SpatioTemporal Reasoning In Driving Edge Cases), an object-centric benchmark for long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios. STRIDE covers six task families: spatial perception, spatial understanding, temporal memory, temporal extrapolation, trajectory prediction, and scene-context awareness. It pairs multiple-choice questions probing individual spatiotemporal judgments with related free-form visual question answering (VQA) requiring detailed scene explanations and justifications of driving decisions. We prioritize scenes with unusual object behaviors and complex traffic interactions, generate reference answers from structured dataset annotations through automated procedures, and use limited language-model assistance and human verification to ensure annotation quality. Across 12 proprietary, open-weight, and driving-specialized models, even the best performer, GPT-6-Astra, achieves only 43.4% average multiple-choice accuracy, versus an approximately 20% random-choice baseline. Further analysis reveals that strong performance in describing driving scenes does not necessarily translate to accurate safety-critical judgments, and that models struggle more with reconstructing object motion than recalling past positions. STRIDE thus exposes spatiotemporal driving limitations that aggregate VQA scores can conceal.
items.author: Lieqi Liu, Rui gao, Jia-Chen Gu, Wenbo Hu, Zhaobin Mo, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar, Wei Wang, Nanyun Peng
items.summary: STRIDE is an object-centric benchmark for evaluating VLM spatiotemporal reasoning in long-tail, safety-critical driving scenarios, spanning six task families including spatial perception, temporal memory, and temporal extrapolation. It addresses the gap where existing benchmarks test edge cases with basic perception questions or simple temporal scenarios.

items.title: Not All Actions Contribute Equally: Learning Precise Progress Estimation from Imprecise Demonstrations
items.content: arXiv:2610.23769v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Progress estimators play an essential role in providing dense reward signals for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation, but accurately assessing task progress can be much challenging. Existing methods heavily rely on expert data and naively assume that all actions within a demonstration contribute to task success. This assumption often breaks down in real-world scenarios, especially in high-precision manipulation, where subtle geometric errors can lead to task failure. Therefore, these methods can erroneously interpret human mistakes as meaningful progress, further corrupting progress learning. We argue that a key limitation is the lack of a global prior regarding task evaluation criteria, which is crucial for distinguishing meaningful progress from human mistakes. To this end, we propose PRIME, a novel progress estimator capable of learning precise progress estimation from imprecise demonstrations by aggregating experience across trajectories. PRIME constructs a weighted graph over observed states, connecting states across trajectories based on spatial proximity and visual consistency. Edge weights encode spatial distances as transition costs, and shortest-path search approximates the geodesic distance to success. Changes in this distance naturally distinguish advancement, stagnation, and setbacks without assuming monotonic progress over time. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real world on precise manipulation tasks show that PRIME is consistently effective across diverse tasks, and robust to data with varying degrees of suboptimality. Notably, the advantage of PRIME gets more pronounced in higher-precision scenarios, yielding up to a \(5\times\) improvement in policy success rate over the SFT baselines on charger insertion.
items.author: Huanqian Wang, Boshi Tang, Botong Xiao, Jie Zhang, Yang Yue, Danhua Tao, Shiji Song, Gao Huang
items.summary: This work improves task progress estimation for RL reward shaping by rejecting the assumption that all actions in a demonstration contribute to success, which fails in high-precision manipulation where subtle errors cause failure. It injects a global prior about task evaluation criteria, likely leveraging foundation models, to distinguish meaningful progress from human mistakes in imperfect demonstrations.
items.reasoning: Learning from imprecise demonstrations is a persistent practical bottleneck, and the critique of naive progress estimators is well founded with clear relevance to dense-reward RL for precision tasks. The idea is solid but the framing builds incrementally on existing progress-estimation and demonstration-noise literature, yielding a good rather than exceptional score.

Notably, the advantage of PRIME gets more pronounced in higher-precision scenarios, yielding up to a \(5\times\) improvement in policy success rate over the SFT baselines on charger insertion.

items.title: Where Latents Belong and How They Flow: Joint Identification of Structural Roles
items.content: arXiv:2610.23074v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Latent factors in dynamical systems can play different roles across observations and time. For example, an idea in a group meeting may be expressed by only some participants, inherit information from earlier discussions, and shape what is said next. We formalize this notion as the structural role of a latent factor, describing where it is expressed, whether it receives influence from the past, and whether it transmits influence to the future. The main challenge is correspondence, since the three structures may be identified under different permutations, while a structural role is defined only when they are aligned to the same latent coordinate. We show that, under suitable structural and variability conditions, all three roles are jointly identifiable under a common permutation at each time point. Guided by this theory, we develop RoleTrace, a framework that traces structural roles in a shared latent coordinate system. Synthetic experiments validate structural recovery, while experiments on multiparty meetings examine the identified roles in real sequential interactions.

items.summary: This work formalizes the structural role of latent factors in dynamical systems — where they are expressed, whether they inherit influence from the past, and whether they transmit influence forward — and addresses the correspondence problem of aligning these structures to the same latent coordinate. Under suitable conditions, all three roles can be jointly identified, with an estimation method proposed.
items.reasoning: Conceptually novel identifiability theory with ties to causal representation learning (Kun Zhang co-author); intellectually strong, though immediate applications are less direct.

items.title: A Stronger Teacher Within: Strengthening MoE Models via On-Policy Bidirectional Distillation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23185v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLMs, but its outcome-level rewards provide only sparse supervision. On-Policy Distillation offers dense token-level feedback, yet requires a stronger compatible teacher, while on-policy self-distillation relies on hand-designed privileged information. We observe that the MoE architecture itself offers a way to resolve this dilemma, as increasing the activation budget per token exposes latent expert capacity and yields a potentially stronger teacher within the model. However, naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together. We therefore propose MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework following a recovery-then-improvement strategy: we first restore the activation-expanded high-$k$ model and further strengthen it by exploiting its additional active capacity, then reverse the direction of distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back into the original low-$k$ configuration, retaining its inference-time activation budget. Across diverse MoE models and benchmarks, MoEvolve improves the initial models by up to $22.2$ domain-average points and outperforms same-budget RLVR baselines by up to $6.5$ points. Notably, the final low-$k$ models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers.

items.summary: MoEvolve exploits the MoE architecture itself as a self-teacher by increasing the per-token expert activation budget to expose latent expert capacity, using bidirectional on-policy distillation to make newly co-activated experts work together. This avoids requiring an external stronger teacher for dense token-level feedback during RLVR training.
items.reasoning: Clever architectural insight that MoE capacity expansion can serve as an internal teacher for distillation; relevant to MoE training practice, though empirical validation scope is unclear from the abstract.

items.title: RTSM: Adapting Recursive Models to Multivariate Time-Series Classification
items.content: arXiv:2610.23353v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate multivariate time-series classification requires extracting temporal features and integrating information across a sequence. Weight-tied refinement offers a way to repeatedly process these features without allocating new parameters at each stage. Applying this principle to time series requires choosing both a temporal representation and a latent-state organization suited to classification. We introduce the Recursive Time-Series Model (RTSM), which combines a learned convolutional temporal tokenizer, single-state weight-tied refinement, and a pooled classification readout. Across all 30 UEA datasets, RTSM achieves 72.81% mean accuracy under validation-based configuration and checkpoint selection, the highest observed mean among the 17 evaluated deep-learning models and 1.60 percentage points above MambaSL. Ablations on eight datasets favor the proposed tokenizer over a simple convolutional embedding and the single-state model over the tested two-state variants. The complete classifier reaches 86.10% mean accuracy versus 84.79% for a separately trained tokenizer-only classifier. These findings identify temporal encoding and state organization as key design choices for adapting recursive architectures to time series. The resulting classifier combines competitive accuracy with a shared refinement module whose parameter count is independent of computational depth.

This demonstrates that parameter-efficient recursive architectures can be competitive in the time-series domain.

items.title: Bridging Compressed Communication and Local Steps via Spectral Method in Federated Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23434v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of complex models across large-scale networks of edge devices while keeping data localized. However, data heterogeneity and high communication overhead remain fundamental bottlenecks. Recently, the spectral optimizer Muon has demonstrated remarkable advantages over Adam-like methods in centralized training. While recent efforts have attempted to transition Muon to FL, naive integrations into traditional architectures fail short. Crucially, existing approaches do not support the the communication compression and local steps --- the two foundational techniques of efficient FL. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel spectral FL method that utilizes both local updates and compression. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees under mild assumptions, notably eliminating the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition. Empirical evaluation on standard image classification benchmarks validates the efficiency and robustness of our approach.
items.author: Dmitriy Bystrov, George Chirkov, Daniil Medyakov, Dmitry Bylinkin, Aleksandr Beznosikov
items.summary: This paper introduces a spectral federated learning method based on the Muon optimizer that supports both communication compression and local updates, the two foundational efficiency techniques of FL that prior Muon-based FL approaches lacked. It tackles data heterogeneity and communication overhead simultaneously. The work connects a hot centralized optimizer trend to practical distributed training constraints.
items.reasoning: Timely integration of Muon into federated settings with both key FL techniques supported; solid theory-practice combination, but impact hinges on Muon's long-term standing versus Adam-family optimizers.

items.title: Deep LLM layers expose passage-level context in EEG during silent reading
items.content: arXiv:2610.23638v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In a previous report we showed that a decoder can recover open-vocabulary word-level information from 19-channel EEG recorded during silent reading, by aligning short EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings of the presented word taken from a large language model (LLM). That analysis contrasted two of the model's 33 layers: the context-free input embedding and one mid-depth layer. Here we ask how EEG-decodable structure is distributed over the full depth of the language model. We trained one decoder per layer of Llama-3.1-8B, with and without a causal transformer over the sequence of EEG windows. We distinguish word-level decodability from a context-tracking component. Word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines steadily towards the last layer. In contrast, the context-tracking component of the retrieval gain rises with depth, both with and without a causal transformer. Unexpectedly, a decoder that sees a single 0.5-s window at a time tracks the text passage too. Two new controls dissect this component. A target-geometry control, a synthetic predictor made of the true target plus noise calibrated to each decoder's word-level accuracy, shows that context tracking is not a by-product of word decoding and target geometry. A control that permutes predictions across runs from either the same or from different sessions shows that most of the observed context-tracking is not caused by an EEG recording session signature. Instead, context tracking mostly follows the text. A single EEG window therefore carries passage-level information that a contextual target can absorb. The results locate word identity in the early layers of the language model, discourse state in the deeper layers, and make the choice of target layer a design dial for EEG language decoders.

items.summary: The authors decode open-vocabulary information from 19-channel EEG during silent reading by aligning EEG windows with hidden-state embeddings from Llama-3.1-8B, training one decoder per layer. They find word-level decodability peaks in early layers and declines toward deeper layers, while deeper layers expose passage-level contextual structure. This maps how LLM internal representations correspond to neural signals, with implications for brain-computer interfaces and computational neuroscience.
items.reasoning: An interesting neural-representational study using a well-known existing model (Llama-3.1-8B, long established by the coverage date) to probe how contextual information surfaces in brain signals. The layer-wise analysis is a genuine contribution, though EEG decoding at 19 channels has inherent ceiling constraints.

items.title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
items.content: arXiv:2610.21713v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.
items.author: Linda Bekov\'a, Rodrigo Alves
items.summary: The authors show that item embeddings used in recommender systems can leak item identities via a simple cosine-similarity attack when an adversary holds auxiliary item text, across language models and two real-world datasets. Leakage further propagates to user re-identification from sparse ratings, revealing an underappreciated privacy risk.
items.reasoning: A practically important privacy finding with a simple, reproducible attack method, though the technique itself is straightforward and the contribution is mainly in demonstrating and characterizing the risk.

items.title: Embodiment-Classifier Guidance: Transferring Frozen VLAs Across Robot Dynamics without Demonstrations
items.content: arXiv:2610.22576v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Flow-based policies such as $\pi_0$ are trained on a fixed set of embodiments, and transferring them to new ones is an open problem. To adapt a frozen $\pi_0$ to a new embodiment without additional demonstrations or parameter updates, we train a lightweight embodiment classifier to distinguish successful action chunks on the source body from those on the target body, using a few calibration tasks. On transfer tasks that $\pi_0$ saw on its source body but the classifier was never trained on, we nudge each denoising step of $\pi_0$ with the classifier's gradient, which estimates the direction from the distribution of successful actions on the source body toward that on the target body. On the LIBERO simulation benchmark with four modified controllers, embodiment-classifier guidance raises $\pi_0$'s average success on the target bodies from 72% to 80% across 12 suite-controller pairs, with a 31% relative reduction in failures (11 of 12 gain; 5 significant after Holm correction). In simulation, guidance is data-efficient, needing few target-body rollouts per task, which makes it promising for sim-to-real transfer, where rollouts are costly. Guidance is mixed on weak wrists and harmful on a locked wrist, when the classifier lacks data or favors infeasible motions. Collecting more target-body data with guided $\pi_0$ can fill such gaps: on one weak-wrist arm, guided $\pi_0$ solved a task on which unguided $\pi_0$ had zero successes in the original data, and retraining the classifier on the guided successes raised success from 52.5% to 70.7%.

Classifier gradients nudge each denoising step toward the target body's distribution of successful actions, validated on LIBERO with modified controller configurations.

items.title: Causal Edit Serialization
items.content: arXiv:2610.22820v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Standard autoregressive language models generate text sequentially, but revision requires referring back to tokens in the input context or those already generated. Causal Edit Serialization (CES) is introduced as a framework for expressing such revisions within the same causal token stream. Special pointer tokens are paired with predicted source addresses, allowing insertion, deletion, replacement, copying and movement to be localized explicitly. A lightweight localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support both address prediction and conditioning on previously emitted pointers, while retaining a standard causal attention mask. A pretraining procedure combines ordinary language modeling with serialized repairs derived from random corruptions, model-generated edits and repeated text. Across model scales and editing baselines, CES models demonstrate complete applied edits with modestly higher clean-text bits per byte than clean autoregressive models. Supervised and reinforcement-learning post-training provide a grammatical-error-correction proof of concept, producing more beneficial than harmful changes under reference-blind model judging. Correct repair programs also improve subsequent text prediction while the original context and its cached states are retained. CES provides a common interface for generation and localized revision, with potential extensions to iterative refinement and additional pointer-addressed transformations.

A localization head and dual-index rotary position encoding support address prediction while preserving a standard causal attention mask, with pretraining mixing language modeling and serialized repair tasks.
items.reasoning: A novel architectural idea addressing a real limitation of purely sequential autoregression, namely structured revision without breaking causality. The design is technically clean; impact depends on whether the pretraining recipe yields measurable gains, which the abstract does not fully establish.

items.title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks
items.content: arXiv:2610.23322v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. Corresponding deep learning methods are developed as bundles: a new architecture together with a new training loss, tested on one to five datasets against a handful of baselines. Thus, a state-of-the-art result cannot be attributed to the architecture, the loss, or the evaluation protocol. The coupling is not accidental: with one incidence curve per cause, a network's head is tied to the losses expressible on it. We vary the two axes independently, three losses, two of them strictly proper, on four backbones, across two modalities that tease the axes apart: 20 tabular and 3 pathology-image datasets. One loss wins in both: modelling cumulative incidence directly under censoring weighting. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. This is an avenue of progress: composed, the two give a model nobody has tried, RealMLP or TabM trained with the cumulative-incidence loss, which takes the best Brier score in our benchmark.
items.author: Julie Alberge, Ga\"el Varoquaux, Judith Ab\'ecassis
items.summary: This paper disentangles the coupled contributions of architecture and loss in deep survival analysis with competing risks, where prior work bundles new heads with new losses. Varying three losses (two strictly proper) across four backbones and two modalities, it provides an attribution of what actually drives state-of-the-art results.
items.reasoning: A careful ablation study in the Inria/Varoquaux tradition of rigorous ML methodology, addressing a real reproducibility problem in healthcare ML where architecture and loss are confounded. Findings should guide future competing-risks model design; impact is moderate but the methodological lesson generalizes.

items.title: HardEval: An Execution-Verified Benchmark for AI-Driven Security Hardening and Compliance Remediation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23685v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open-weight configurations, multi-run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.
items.author: Manohar Vellala, Soumya Banerjee, Sandip Roy, Ross Gore, Sachin Shetty
items.summary: HardEval is an execution-verified benchmark evaluating whether language-model agents can translate natural-language STIG security requirements into persistent OS configuration changes across SSH, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. items.content_html: arXiv:2610.23685v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Implementing Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG) controls remains a demanding operating-system administration task. Each natural-language security requirement must be translated into a precise and persistent configuration change. These changes span Secure Shell (SSH) configuration, authentication policy, audit rules, and kernel parameters. Existing benchmarks do not measure whether a model can perform this task on a live system. Code benchmarks evaluate isolated programs without persistent system state, while agent benchmarks largely focus on applications rather than operating-system configuration. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{HardEval}, an execution-verified benchmark for evaluating language-model-assisted security hardening. HardEval is built from Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 STIG controls that fail on an unhardened baseline system. Expert-written reference remediations and Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language (OVAL) checks serve as hidden ground truth for grading; they are never shown to the model, and each task states only the required security outcome while withholding the implementation. The model produces a Bash script, which is executed on a live virtual machine and graded from fail to pass using the corresponding OpenSCAP/OVAL compliance check. Evaluation of fourteen frontier and open-weight configurations reveals large and uneven capability differences across security domains. A recurring failure mode is plausible security code that does not satisfy the exact compliance condition. For four open-weight configurations, multi-run Wilson confidence intervals preserve the observed ordering. HardEval is publicly available.

items.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
items.content: arXiv:2610.23821v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

items.title: The Model Knows Better: Defending Medical Multi-Agent Systems Against Prompt Injection
items.content: arXiv:2610.22594v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Medical multi-agent systems, in which LLM agents discuss a case, are increasingly studied for clinical decision support. Prompt injection, text that an attacker adds to a model's input, can manipulate LLMs into wrong decisions. How it affects these systems, and how to protect them, remains unclear. Across two systems, two model families and three benchmarks, a single injected passage succeeds in up to 61% of cases, and collaboration does not consistently protect against it. Existing defenses help only partly: they miss injections that look like ordinary clinical text. Yet when asked to check the injected text against the patient's findings, a model that followed the injection usually rejects it. We therefore propose a training-free defense that verifies the clinical judgments behind the system's decision. Following clinical practice, it separates the patient's findings from clinical judgments, such as diagnoses, recommendations and instructions, and checks each judgment against the findings alone, so the decision rests only on supported judgments. Our defense outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, lowering attack success on MedQA to 4-7% while maintaining accuracy on cases without an attack, and remains effective with a medical model and against defense-aware and adaptive attacks.
items.author: Fardin Ahsan Sakib, Ziwei Zhu, Ozlem Uzuner
items.summary: Shows that a single injected passage manipulates medical multi-agent LLM systems in up to 61% of cases and that agent collaboration does not reliably protect against it. The paper proposes a training-free defense that asks the model to check injected text against patient findings, exploiting the observation that a model which followed an injection usually rejects it on verification.
items.reasoning: Prompt injection in high-stakes multi-agent medical settings is an important safety problem, and the empirical attack success rates plus the insight that models can self-correct when prompted to verify against evidence are valuable. The defense is training-free and practical, though evaluated on limited benchmarks.

items.title: On the Position Bias of Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Study
items.content: arXiv:2610.22807v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.

items.summary: A comprehensive study of position bias in LLMs spanning model scales from billion to trillion parameters, multiple-choice and multi-document tasks, and five languages, showing bias remains pronounced at small scale while shrinking (with nuances) for frontier models. It extends understanding of a vulnerability that undermines multiple-choice evaluation integrity and RAG reliability.
items.reasoning: Useful, broad empirical audit of a well-known problem with unusually wide coverage of scales and languages, informing evaluation methodology and RAG reliability. However, it is primarily a measurement study of a documented phenomenon rather than a novel method or causal insight.

items.title: KiranaBench: Can a Language Model Run a Neighbourhood Shop?
items.content: arXiv:2610.22980v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on long-horizon tasks, including autonomously running a business. Existing benchmarks for this setting are almost exclusively English-language, Western in retail context, and single-agent, with the agent observing the business directly. We study how these results transfer to a multi-agent Indic setting. We introduce KiranaBench, a simulated Indian general store in which four roles (manager, cashier, helper, and bookkeeper) are each played by a separate LLM agent. Interactions with customers and suppliers occur in English, Hindi, or Hinglish, and product demand is calibrated to India's national Household Consumption Expenditure Survey. Evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that all fall far short of a fixed-rule shopkeeper baseline: the best model earns only one-eighth of the baseline's profit, and two models finish below an unmanaged shop. Performance is also consistently lower for Hindi and Hinglish than for English supplier communication. KiranaBench offers evidence that current LLM agents are not yet reliable for autonomously operating small businesses in India, and provides a testbed for developing agents suited to settings that are long-horizon, collaborative, and multilingual.

items.title: MGE-PO: Entropy-Aware Credit Assignment for Mathematical Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23245v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: GRPO assigns the same group-relative advantage to equally rewarded responses within a question, leaving their generation uncertainty unused. We introduce MGE-PO, centered on four-quadrant (4Q) advantage shaping that combines verified correctness with rollout generation entropy. Correctness determines the sign of an additional correction, while entropy controls its magnitude: lower-entropy successes receive larger bonuses and higher-entropy failures receive larger penalties. An online entropy-based question curriculum supports this credit rule using cached rollout measurements. At the final checkpoint after eight training epochs on Qwen3-8B-Base, adding 4Q across three policy optimization settings yields absolute gains of 3.23-3.69% in six-benchmark macro avg@32 and 4.24-11.06% in macro pass@32. On Qwen2.5-7B-Base, the complete configuration raises four-benchmark macro avg@32 from 41.5% to 45.4%.

items.summary: MGE-PO improves on GRPO for RL-based math reasoning by using four-quadrant advantage shaping that combines verified correctness with rollout generation entropy: low-entropy successes get larger bonuses and high-entropy failures larger penalties. An online entropy-based question curriculum uses cached rollout measurements. On Qwen3-8B-Base it yields absolute gains of roughly 3.23-3.69% across settings.
items.reasoning: A concrete, empirically validated improvement to widely used GRPO-style policy optimization with a clean intuition about entropy-aware credit assignment. Gains are solid but incremental within a crowded area of RLVR research.

items.title: VISTA: Steering LLMs with Latent User Values Inferred from a Few Survey Answers
items.content: arXiv:2610.23702v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a person values, which stays largely consistent across tasks. Yet most methods either learn task-specific preferences or place the user's profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. We introduce VISTA (Value-Informed Steering and Targeted Acquisition), which infers a latent profile from users' (full or partial) survey answers, and maps the profile through a hypernetwork to a user-specific steering intervention in a frozen LLM to select answer choices or generate free-text responses. Given the same evidence, VISTA matches or beats in-context profiles on synthetic preferences (Food2D), the World Values Survey (WVS), and PrimeX, without adding prompt tokens. To reduce the cognitive burden of completing full surveys, VISTA also chooses which questions to ask and when to stop: on WVS it stops after 6% of the questionnaire while retaining 94% of the full-history gain, where standard adaptive testing retains at most 42%. The dominant steering direction is an interpretable value axis on which VISTA places unseen users accurately. Our results point toward pluralistic alignment that adapts to individuals at deployable cost.

items.title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations
items.content: arXiv:2610.22708v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.
items.author: Nicholas Saban, Charvi Bannur, Mariya Vasileva, Darshan Deshpande
items.summary: GlobeBench is the first standardized benchmark for text-based world models, with 1,632 tasks across five domains and nineteen simulation skills that test whether models can predict environment responses to actions given full agent trajectories. It enables systematic comparison and improvement of models intended to simulate RL environment state transitions.
items.reasoning: Fills a genuine evaluation gap for an emerging research direction (text-based world models for RL simulation) with broad task coverage; importance will grow if the community adopts it, but it is a benchmark paper without headline results.

items.title: Sep-Latent: Separator Tokens as Natural Compression Anchors for Implicit Reasoning
items.content: arXiv:2610.22924v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in complex reasoning through explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT), but the associated computational overhead and token verbosity remain significant barriers to efficiency. While implicit reasoning in continuous latent spaces offers a promising alternative, existing methods like Coconut and CODI often rely on fixed-length latent sequences and suffer from representational collapse. In this paper, we propose Sep-Latent, an adaptive implicit reasoning framework that utilizes separator tokens as structural semantic anchors. By introducing an Attention-Decay mechanism, we force the model to aggregate and compress reasoning logic into these anchors during training. We then align explicit and implicit pathways through multi-level distillation across all layers to ensure logical consistency. Crucially, Sep-Latent enables dynamic reasoning depth by adaptively terminating the latent thinking phase based on query complexity. Experimental results on the GSM8k-Aug benchmark show that Sep-Latent achieves an accuracy of 56.8\% with an average of only 5.4 tokens, significantly outperforming prior fixed-length implicit models in efficiency while narrowing the performance gap with explicit CoT. Further analysis via PCA and symbolic variant testing confirms that our method ensures semantic grounding and exhibits superior robustness to perturbations.

items.title: ScoutRoute: Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Routing Using Internal Language Model Signals
items.content: arXiv:2610.23443v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Efficient expert routing is a fundamental challenge in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems, particularly for heterogeneous collections of independently trained Large Language Mod els (LLMs). Existing routing approaches typically rely on jointly trained gating networks, prompt-based predictors, or computationally expensive multi-model inference, limiting their flexibility and efficiency. This paper presents ScoutRoute, a lightweight post-hoc routing framework that predicts expert competence using internal language model signals extracted from a single forward pass through an inexpensive scout model. Hidden-state representations are used to estimate cross-model competence through lightweight logistic probes, while logit-derived confidence measures are incorporated within a domain-aware routing strategy for efficient expert selec tion without modifying the underlying language models. ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models
items.author: Rajdeep Pandhare, Delzaan Bharucha
items.summary: ScoutRoute is a lightweight post-hoc routing framework for heterogeneous MoE-style collections of independently trained LLMs. It predicts expert competence from a single forward pass through a cheap scout model, using hidden-state probes and logit-derived confidence measures rather than jointly trained gates or expensive multi-model inference. This enables efficient routing without retraining the routed experts.
items.reasoning: Routing among independently trained models is an interesting and increasingly relevant problem as multi-model deployments proliferate. The approach is elegant and efficient, but the work appears to come from a smaller team and the abstract does not indicate which baselines or scale of evaluation were used.

ScoutRoute isevaluatedon fiveopen-weightlanguagemodels across fourbenchmark datasets covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, commonsense reasoning, and multidis ciplinary knowledge. Experimental results show that ScoutRoute consistently outperforms individual routing signals while requiring only a single scout-model inference. The proposed competence probes also achieve superior calibration compared with conventional confidence measures, demonstrating that internal language model representations provide transferable information for accurate and efficient expert routing across heterogeneous language models

items.title: Beyond the Benchmark: Conditioning, Domains and Failure Modes of Qwen3-TTS
items.content: arXiv:2610.23678v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Qwen3-TTS reports state-of-the-art zero-shot voice cloning, but its technical report leaves open how the model should be conditioned, how it behaves outside read speech, and how it fails. We characterise its two cloning interfaces, in-context learning (ICL) and X-Vector, against Chatterbox, XTTS-v2 and F5-TTS on read, meeting, emotional and air-traffic-control (ATC) speech, using eighteen objective measures, an LLM judge, a spoofing countermeasure and a listening test. Neither interface dominates: ICL clones timbre more closely from correctly transcribed references, X-Vector clones timing, and ICL degrades sharply when a short reference transcript is wrong. Domain explains four times more variance than system choice. Qwen3-TTS leads on intelligibility and pitch register but trails on prosody, and the objective measures rank systems differently from listeners. An off-the-shelf countermeasure flags its clones no more often than genuine recordings, and on ATC radio it fails for every system. Code and audio are released.

items.title: FlashControl: One-Step Controllable Generator via Distillation-Friendly Single-Stream Teachers
items.content: arXiv:2610.22537v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Diffusion models have become a leading approach in visual generative modeling, particularly effective in text-to-image and controllable generation. Their main drawback is slow inference as it requires many sampling steps. While recent distillation methods enable one-step text-to-image generation, extending these techniques to controllable generation is still challenging. Existing controllable models, such as ControlNet, rely on dual-branch design that make distillation difficult. In this work, we adopt a simpler strategy. Instead of adding extra conditional branches, we finetune a selected subset of layers in the original text-to-image diffusion model to directly enable controllable generation. This results in DeltaControl, a single-flow, multi-step diffusion model capable of supporting spatial-condition generation while matching the performance of dual-branch approaches. Building on this teacher model, we further apply step-distillation to obtain FlashControl, a one-step model capable of spatial controllable generation with a single forward pass.
items.author: Ngan Nguyen, Dung Nguyen, Quan Dao, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Minh Hoai, Cuong Pham, Anh Tran
items.summary: The paper tackles the difficulty of distilling controllable diffusion generators like ControlNet into fast one-step models by replacing dual-branch conditional architectures with a single-stream teacher. Instead of adding extra branches, DeltaControl finetunes a subset of layers in the original text-to-image diffusion model to enable controllability directly, making the resulting teacher far more distillation-friendly. This yields FlashControl, a one-step controllable generator that preserves spatial conditioning while drastically reducing inference cost.
items.reasoning: The insight that dual-branch designs are the obstacle to distilling controllable generators, and that single-stream finetuned teachers solve it, is a meaningful efficiency contribution with clear practical value for real-time controllable image generation. The academic team (including Metaxas) is credible, but the work targets a niche within diffusion research and one-step distillation is an active, crowded area, capping its comparative impact.

items.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
items.content: arXiv:2610.22700v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.

items.summary: Cambrian-BEV extends the Cambrian-S video MLLM with a parameter-free geometric tokenization that back-projects patch features into a shared bird's-eye-view frame using depth and camera pose, giving embodied agents a persistent spatial context. items.reasoning: A clean, training-light geometric modification to visual tokenization with a clear motivation for embodied spatial reasoning. Building on the established Cambrian-S model strengthens credibility, though the evaluation breadth is not fully evident from the abstract.

items.title: TriFold: Folding irregular 3D Gaussians into structured latents for 3D Scene Generation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23050v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent progress in 3D generation has motivated growing interest in compact generative representations of complex 3D scenes. For native 3D Gaussian scenes, however, learning such representations remains challenging due to widely varying primitive counts, nonuniform spatial density, and differences in geometry and appearance even among spatially neighboring primitives. In this work, we introduce TriFold, a native 3D Gaussian VAE that encodes Gaussian scenes into a fixed-layout triplane latent and jointly reconstructs their geometry and appearance. The key insight is to impose structural regularity on the latent space while preserving the spatial adaptivity of the underlying Gaussians. During encoding, we use cell-wise learned queries to aggregate projected Gaussians into multiple slots per cell, reducing the information loss caused by single-feature pooling. During decoding, occupancy prediction identifies active regions, where query-based set prediction and candidate selection reconstruct local Gaussian sets with spatially varying primitive counts. Building on this representation, we train a latent flow-matching model for conditional scene-level 3DGS generation, enabling point-cloud-conditioned synthesis and single-image-conditioned amodal generation. Experiments demonstrate that TriFold achieves high-fidelity reconstruction and generation from a single image that provides only a partial observation of the scene, validating its effectiveness for native 3D Gaussian representation learning. https://fantasy-amap.github.io/TriFold

The key contribution is imposing structural regularity on the latent space while preserving the spatial adaptivity of Gaussians, addressing varying primitive counts and nonuniform density. This enables more compact generative representations for complex 3D scene generation.
items.reasoning: A solid architectural contribution addressing a genuine bottleneck in generative 3D representations. The triplane-latent VAE for native Gaussians could become a useful building block for downstream 3D generative models, though results are not fully visible.

items.title: SCALE: Improving Guidance-Free Visual Generation via Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23263v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) is essential for improving sample quality in visual generation, but it incurs substantial sampling overhead. Existing guidance-free approaches halve this cost by approximating the CFG with a single model inference, but their performance is bounded by the CFG and inherits its limitations. In this paper, we propose self-contrastive guidance (SCG), which contrasts the model's prediction on real and self-generated samples to obtain a direct, model-based signal that pushes generation toward the true data manifold. Integrating SCG into the standard likelihood objective via reparameterization yields Self-Contrastive Alignment for Likelihood Estimation (SCALE), a guidance-free training framework that produces SCG-enhanced predictions in a single forward pass. Across class-conditional and text-to-image generation on diffusion and autoregressive models, SCALE consistently outperforms CFG-mimicking guidance-free baselines and improves further when combined with DPO, demonstrating that the self-contrastive signal yields gains complementary to both CFG and preference-based fine-tuning.

Integrated into the likelihood objective via reparameterization, this yields a guidance-free training framework producing SCG-enhanced models. The approach goes beyond prior guidance-free methods that merely approximate CFG and inherit its limitations.

items.title: LithoWorld: An Endpoint World Model for Lithography Process-Window Recovery
items.content: arXiv:2610.23408v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Lithography process drift can move a fabricated pattern outside its process window, producing unqualified scanning electron microscopy (SEM) morphology. We present LithoWorld, an endpoint world model for SEM-guided parameter recovery. Interior representative targets jointly determine qualified reference appearance and correction supervision. A causal predictive branch aligns currentimage features with endpoint representations, while a conditional flow policy generates a two-dimensional correction as an action chunk. The model learns from 173 groups of measured SEMs organized as focus-exposure maps, preserving unmeasured cells as unknown. On 200 test pairs from the 73-group subset, LithoWorld achieves 88.5% qualified-region success and 46.0% interior success, exceeding the strongest comparison method by 2.5 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablations separate the effects of target selection, endpoint alignment, and output parameterization. Qualitative SEM retrieval illustrates recovery to qualified interiors without requiring exact reference-coordinate matching.

items.summary: LithoWorld applies world-model ideas to semiconductor lithography, learning to recover process parameters when drift pushes fabricated patterns outside their process window, guided by SEM imagery. It achieves 88.5 percent qualified-region success on a 200-pair test set, a notable result for manufacturing AI.

items.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
items.content: arXiv:2610.23841v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.

The method adds explicit goal grounding, achieving state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks, and also corrects annotation defects in those benchmarks.

items.title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
items.content: arXiv:2610.23288v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.

items.title: Generative Value Classifier
items.content: arXiv:2610.22497v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Q-learning is premised on learning a function to predict the value of a state-action pair, with the goal of using such a function to guide policy improvement. Most approaches learn this function from scratch using scalar or distributional return targets. This discriminative approach leaves another source of supervision for learning representations unused: the actions themselves. Rather than directly predict the return of a state-action pair, we ask the reverse question: how likely is the action under each possible return? This perspective provides a critic whose generative component is a return-conditioned policy, which can share the actor's architecture. Training this policy supervises the critic with every action rather than with returns alone, and a squared-error loss anchors the critic's Q-value to the bootstrapped target. We evaluate our approach on both offline and online RL tasks and show gains over leading discriminative methods, including distributional RL methods.

This supervises the critic with every action rather than only return targets, providing an additional representation-learning signal.

Practical gains and scalability beyond the evaluated settings remain to be seen, but the idea could influence off-policy RL design.

items.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
items.content: arXiv:2610.22794v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132.
