items.title: ODSS-Net: Orthogonally Decoupled Shared-Specific Representations for Multi-Modal Object Re-Identification
items.content: arXiv:2610.22922v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-modal object re-identification (ReID) leverages complementary information from heterogeneous sensors. Cross-modal alignment and fusion remain challenging. Existing methods mainly reduce modality gaps via feature alignment and fusion. However, alignment may entangle modality-shared structural information with modality-specific cues, while conventional fusion may not fully exploit complementary information. To address these issues, we propose ODSS-Net, a framework for orthogonally decoupled shared-specific representation learning and adaptive fusion of complementary modality-specific features. First, a Shared Structural Feature Construction (SSFC) module suppresses modality-dependent appearance variations and extracts modality-shared structural information. Then, an Orthogonal Specific Feature Learning (OSFL) module aggregates identity-relevant local information and removes the shared-aligned component via geometric orthogonal projection. Finally, a Sample Adaptive Mixture of Experts (SAMoE) module uses the shared structure as routing context to adaptively refine and fuse modality-specific features. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ODSS-Net for multi-modal object ReID.
items.author: Zhifeng Ma, Yuhong Feng, Chongyi Huang, Mingyang Zhou, Minwen Deng
items.summary: ODSS-Net addresses multi-modal object re-identification by orthogonally decoupling modality-shared structural features from modality-specific cues and adaptively fusing complementary specific features. Modules include Shared Structural Feature Construction to suppress modality-dependent appearance variations.
items.reasoning: A reasonable architectural contribution to multi-modal ReID, a fairly specialized subfield; the shared-specific decomposition idea is sensible but variants of this pattern are common in the literature.
items.summary_html: ODSS-Net addresses multi-modal object re-identification by orthogonally decoupling modality-shared structural features from modality-specific cues and adaptively fusing complementary specific features. items.title: A Paired RGB-Sonar Dataset for Fish Monitoring with Consumer Sonar
items.content: arXiv:2610.23759v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Imaging sonar enables underwater observation in conditions where optical imaging is ineffective due to darkness and turbid water. However, imaging-sonar systems previously used for ecological monitoring have typically been expensive, limiting their accessibility. Consumer forward-looking sonar has the potential to make fish monitoring more accessible, but its noisy imagery makes annotation and the development of automated methods challenging. We introduce the Huntington and Caltech Koi RGB and Sonar dataset (HaCKRS), which pairs Garmin LiveScope imaging-sonar recordings with top-down RGB video of koi carp. The dataset contains more than 105,000 temporally matched frame pairs, spanning approximately 3.3 hours of recordings across four range and orientation configurations. We provide frame-wise metadata, sonar geometry and coordinate information, synchronization data for all four configurations, and planar registration for the three horizontal configurations. The release focuses on paired observations and calibration rather than task-specific fish annotations. We intend HaCKRS to support annotation and the development of fish detection, tracking, and counting methods, and investigations into the potential of consumer sonar for ecological monitoring.

items.title: Pedicel-Targeted Strawberry Harvesting via Imitation Learning on a Low-Cost Teleoperated Robotic Arm
items.content: arXiv:2610.22765v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Precise pedicel-targeted grasping in strawberry harvesting remains a critical bottleneck due to the pedicel's small diameter (1.3-3 mm), color similarity with surrounding foliage, and precise force control required for clean abscission zone detachment. As a market-grade crop, strawberry aesthetic value makes bruise-free pedicel detachment essential over direct fruit grasping. Classical approaches struggle to unify vision models, motion planning, and contact manipulation into a robust framework, particularly in occluded canopy environments. Therefore, this work presents a visuomotor imitation learning pipeline for pedicel-targeted strawberry harvesting that unifies perception, motion planning, and contact manipulation from collecting human teleoperation demonstrations, training an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy with a ResNet-50 visual backbone, and deploying the learned policy autonomously on a Jetson AGX Orin edge platform at 15 Hz. The trained policy achieved consistent loss convergence from 2.84 to 0.091 over 100K gradient steps on 130 demonstrations. We have also established a reproducible open-source pipeline with publicly released dataset and model weights for the agricultural robotics community. Full dataset is available at, https://huggingface.co/datasets/nitindominicrai/strawberry_pedicel_grasp_teleoperation and trained policy at, https://huggingface.co/nitindominicrai/act_strawberry_pedicel. To replicate this work, all code, configurations, and deployment instructions are publicly available at, https://github.com/nitin-dominic/autonomous_strawberry_pedicel_harvesting.

It is built on a low-cost teleoperated arm.

items.title: Quick Thoughts on Overhang Arguments
items.content:
I have two goals for this post:

- Pose the question: Have overhang arguments been used successfully in other fields?
- Lay out some of the reasons why I am suspicious of overhang arguments.

I've had the second of these on my mind for a few years now and am posting something rough rather than leaving it in drafts.

# Intro

Within AI safety, people sometimes use overhang arguments to justify doing things that appear suspicious. The core of an overhang argument, as I see it is:

- We are worried about some particular (dangerous) progress happening very quickly in the future.
- We can push forward at least one of the inputs to that progress today. We expect doing so will both bring the dangerous thing sooner and slow down future progress toward the dangerous thing. We're trying to trade time now for time later.

A common form of this is a "compute overhang" argument: let's avoid situations where there is tons of compute lying around and drastically more efficient algorithms get developed, as that would allow these algorithms to scale rapidly to ASI. Therefore, we should push forward algorithm efficiency as much as we can today (in addition to all of the non-compute inputs) while the compute stock is relatively low, and then progress in the future will be more limited by the rate of growth of compute stock (relatively slow and predictable).

# Have overhang arguments been used successfully in other fields?

Have people made overhang arguments in other fields, have those arguments been compelling, what are the key similarities/differences to AI, and how has that gone? Based on asking LLMs, here are some examples (though all have key disanalogies):...

items.summary: The author questions the widely used overhang argument in AI safety, which justifies accelerating inputs like algorithmic efficiency today to trade current progress for slower future dangerous progress. items.title: How Many, but How Sure? Class Competition as a Confidence Proxy in Multi-Class Density-Based Counting
items.content: arXiv:2610.23611v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-class density estimators can count objects in crowded scenes, but their class-wise outputs offer no indication of how reliably density mass has been allocated. We introduce a training-free confidence proxy based on local competition between the strongest class channels. The resulting prominence measure requires only the predicted density maps, with no retraining or access to model internals. We test whether residual competition is diagnostic of cross-class leakage by attenuating contested density at inference time. On DSACA predictions for the Hicks et al. dataset, this reduces overall MAE from 0.920 to 0.846, suggesting that class competition contains useful information about count reliability.
items.author: Villanelle O'Reilly, Georgios Leontidis, Marc Hanheide
items.summary: This work introduces a training-free confidence proxy for multi-class density-based object counting, based on local competition between the strongest class channels. Attenuating contested density at inference reduces MAE from 0.920 to 0.846 on one dataset, suggesting residual class competition carries useful reliability information. It requires no retraining or access to model internals.
items.reasoning: A neat, lightweight idea for uncertainty estimation in counting models with no retraining cost. However, the empirical evidence appears limited to a single dataset and model (DSACA), so generality is unproven.

We introduce a training-free confidence proxy based on local competition between the strongest class channels. The resulting prominence measure requires only the predicted density maps, with no retraining or access to model internals. We test whether residual competition is diagnostic of cross-class leakage by attenuating contested density at inference time. On DSACA predictions for the Hicks et al. dataset, this reduces overall MAE from 0.920 to 0.846, suggesting that class competition contains useful information about count reliability.

items.title: SAG2: Embedding-Free Multi-Hop Retrieval with BM25 and JEV
items.content: arXiv:2610.22588v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Strong multi-hop retrieval should be practical to deploy without expensive corpus preparation or complex database infrastructure. We present SAG2, an embedding-free retrieval architecture built around a single SQLite database, BM25, and contextual evidence decisions from JEV. SAG2 follows the query-time association principle of SAG (SQL-Retrieval Augmented Generation), while replacing its event-entity and dense indexes with a lexical index over original passages. Selected passages supply terms for further retrieval, and newly retrieved evidence guides subsequent decisions. This moves semantic evidence selection to query time, eliminating offline embedding computation, LLM-based event-entity extraction, and dedicated database servers. The resulting system combines lightweight preparation with strong retrieval accuracy: on 1,000-question subsets of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA, SAG2 achieves the highest Recall@5 and Recall@10 among the compared methods, with Recall@10 of 86.62%, 97.43%, and 99.00%. It also reaches 81.10% document Recall@10 over the 511,962-document EnterpriseRAG-Bench corpus. Indexing all 11,656 MuSiQue passages takes 2.36 seconds, produces a 25.87 MiB database, and requires no model calls. SAG2 demonstrates that accurate multi-hop evidence retrieval can be supported by compact, rapidly prepared infrastructure, making it a practical foundation for knowledge retrieval applications.

items.title: Material and Defocus Cues for Occluded Object Localization in Single Hyperspectral Images: An Exploratory Study
items.content: arXiv:2610.23733v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Partial occlusion makes object detection difficult when visible regions have weak texture or similar appearance. Hyperspectral imaging provides material-dependent spectra and wavelength-dependent optical blur, which offer complementary evidence for separating objects. We investigate a pipeline that combines nonnegative-matrix-factorization-based material grouping, divergence-based optical cues, and graph Laplacian propagation. The propagated scores support region extraction and bounding-box localization without requiring a separate depth sensor at inference. A collection of 30 indoor and six outdoor hyperspectral scenes acquired using two camera systems provides qualitative examples spanning different materials, depth arrangements, and partial occlusions. The examples illustrate how material information can support separation when optical cues are weak, and how optical cues can distinguish some surfaces with similar material properties. Objects sharing both material and depth remain challenging. This exploratory study establishes the sensing rationale and mathematical formulation, while identifying the quantitative evaluation and implementation details needed to assess detection performance systematically.

items.title: Simultaneous Force and Motion Control in Generalised Coordinates
items.content: arXiv:2610.22813v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Robot manipulators often come into contact with rigid objects when performing work. This imposes physical constraints on their motion. Simultaneous force & motion control was developed to regulate contact forces commensurate with these constraints, whilst projecting motion control in to the orthogonal, unconstrained directions. This is typically formulated in the task coordinates, i.e. operational space, then mapped to joint torques to command the robot. However, most constraints on the robot control, such as joint limits, collision avoidance, singularity avoidance, etc. are naturally expressed in generalised coordinates (joint space). Thus, formulating the control problem in task space makes it difficult to guarantee control feasibility. In this paper Gauss' principle of least constraint is used to solve the control as a quadratic programming (QP) problem in generalised coordinates. It is shown that the theoretical solution to this problem produces the correct constrained dynamics for accurate contact force control. Moreover, inequality constraints may be appended to ensure feasibility and safety. Simulation results were conducted in MuJoCo and compared to the operational space formulation. The proposed method is able to simultaneously maintain a desired contact force, minimise trajectory tracking error, and adhere to practical inequality constraints.

items.reasoning: A classical control-theory contribution with a sensible technical argument: constraints are naturally joint-space, so formulating there improves feasibility guarantees. Solid for the control community but foundational rather than headline-grabbing, and single-author work with limited visible empirical scope.

items.title: CGDT-CESN: Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network for Multivariate Time-Series Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2610.22430v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Accurate prediction of multivariate time series requires models that simultaneously capture variable-specific dynamics and cross-variable interactions. In this work, a Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network (CGDT-CESN) is proposed, which comprises a modular reservoir architecture with each cluster distinctly specializing in one of the variables in the multivariate time series. An innovative reservoir design is proposed in which inter-cluster connections are enabled by empirically observed correlations among variables, providing a data-driven coupling mechanism. Apart from conventional readout training, inter-cluster connection weights informed by correlations are trained, which in turn allows the reservoir to capture time-varying cross-variable dependencies without sacrificing computational efficiency and further improves forecasting accuracy. The prediction performance of CGDT-CESN is found to be superior to that of the conventional ESN when evaluated on two fundamentally different datasets: Twitter information cascade evolution and solar wind forecasting. Also, the improvement in performance is preserved across multiple prediction horizons, even when presented with a low volume of data. By unifying cluster-specific specialization with learned inter-variable coupling, CGDT-CESN offers a principled, data-driven route to multivariate time series prediction.

items.title: Partial-Revelation Panel Forecasting: Predictive Information Gain, Allocation, and Coarsening-Consistent Operators
items.content: arXiv:2610.22831v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study partial-revelation panel forecasting: given $k$ of $n$ annotator votes on the previous dialogue turn, predict the full count distribution of the next turn's panel. This cross-turn predictive information differs from same-item annotation value. Under any nested revelation mechanism, the population decrement satisfies $V(k)-V(k+1)=I(Y;R_{k+1}\mid X_k)$; a fitted model also contributes adjacent excess-risk differences. Coarsened-completely-at-random (CCAR) masking supplies the exchangeable random-rater interpretation used in our operators. We define coarsening-consistent panel operators with a closed-form Dirichlet-multinomial realization, learned completion, and rater-count transfer. Against per-level lookup, cold-start count negative log-likelihood differences are -0.422/-0.166/-0.014 nats on IEMOCAP/M3ED/EmoWOZ. A held-out rater experiment measures same-item value: first and second additional votes reduce NLL by 0.583/0.221, 0.578/0.184, and 0.180/0.069 nats, respectively. Cross-turn and same-item gains are not interchangeable, and CCAR masks are controlled interventions rather than observed arrival processes. Consistency is auditable but does not guarantee predictive improvement; per-level marginalization can outperform a shared table. Target-free allocation beats uniform only where row-level signal is predictable: at budget one it recovers 83--93% of retrospective feature class headroom on IEMOCAP/M3ED but does not improve EmoWOZ. Gains are modest and corpus-dependent, with several small or null partial-revelation differences. Code and aggregate result artifacts accompany the preprint.

items.summary: This work studies panel forecasting where only k of n annotator votes from a previous turn are revealed and the model must predict the next turn's full vote-count distribution. It derives information-theoretic identities under nested revelation, defines coarsening-consistent operators with Dirichlet-multinomial realizations, and addresses cold-start and rater-count transfer.
items.reasoning: Careful theoretical treatment of a specific forecasting setting with clean information-theoretic identities, but the problem framing is specialized and broader impact appears limited.

items.title: When Magnitude Suffices: Reconstructing Time-Domain-Gated Microwave Signals Without Phase on a Thoracic Phantom
items.content: arXiv:2610.23608v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Time-domain gating separates the arrivals that form a microwave S-parameter measurement. It requires the measurement of complex values, so this application almost always uses a vector network analyzer (VNA). We show that, on one calibrated measurement configuration, the gated magnitude the VNA would give can be reconstructed from a magnitude-only sweep of a spectrum analyzer with a tracking generator (SA). We select the gate center for separability of the measured states, correct each instrument once by a per-bin subtraction of a reference state, and train a fully connected network on sweeps from both instruments. The test object is a torso phantom with lung-shaped compartments whose filling takes eleven dielectric states, each held out in turn. On $S_{11}$ the reconstruction from SA input reaches a shape error of 0.08 dB$^2$ with a state ordering of 0.81. This matches the reconstruction from VNA input. On $S_{21}$ it reaches 0.82 dB$^2$ and keeps the ordered groups of the states. An explicit phase prediction performs much worse, because gating needs the phase to about 0.2 rad RMS. Across eleven measurement configurations the dependence of phase on magnitude is strong for reflection and weak for transmission. This explains the difference between $S_{11}$ and $S_{21}$. Where the magnitude carries enough of the phase, a scalar instrument gives the gated response without any phase measurement after installation. On the open UM-BMID breast data set, with whole phantoms held out, the shape error of the network is 30 percent lower than that of a per-bin linear map.

items.summary: The authors show that gated magnitude measurements from a vector network analyzer can be reconstructed from magnitude-only spectrum analyzer sweeps using a simple correction scheme and a fully connected network, tested on a torso phantom with eleven dielectric lung states. This could enable cheaper hardware for microwave-based medical sensing. The work sits at the intersection of signal processing, instrumentation, and machine learning.

items.title: GPU-Accelerated Robust MA--RIS Pre-Optimization for Communication and Target Illumination
items.content: arXiv:2610.22431v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Movable antennas (MAs) and reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) offer strong spatial control for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC), but repeatedly adapting MA positions and RIS phases to each channel realization can be impractical. This letter develops a GPU-accelerated robust pre-optimization framework that jointly selects slow-timescale MA geometry and RIS phases and returns a reusable Pareto set balancing expected worst-user rate and transmit-side worst-target illumination. The illumination objective measures directional transmitted power rather than complete echo-detection or parameter-estimation performance. The proposed Regime-Aware Multiobjective Pre-optimization (RAMP) preserves regime-specific Pareto populations, regulates cross-regime mating using Pareto-survival feedback, and constructs a worst-regime robust archive. Numerical results demonstrate competitive robust Pareto quality against the considered evolutionary baselines while avoiding online physical re-optimization.

items.title: One Communicator, Three Vendors: Extending the MoA Predictive Theory to a Real NVIDIA+AMD+CPU MPI Ensemble
items.content: arXiv:2610.22769v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The companion MPI-extension paper validated the first communication-bearing machine-shape ensemble: four NVIDIA A100 ranks and four CPU ranks on one NCSA Delta node under one Open MPI job, reassembled by MPI_Gatherv. This paper extends it to a multi-vendor communicator. A Slurm heterogeneous job spanning Delta's A100 and AMD MI100 partitions places A100, MI100 and CPU ranks (nine in all) under one communicator for the first time. We give the theory (a w_i proportional to 1/t_i weight split for three concurrent realizations; a het-job specification as an admissible directive) and report real results, including what the run exposed: the 1/t split assumes time linear in rows, and this fails for the MI100 rank (6 rows took 597 ms against a linear prediction of 1.6 ms). A launch-geometry model, with predictions recorded before measuring, succeeds for the A100 (time flat from 128 to 3456 rows, stepping at exactly 3520 and 6976) and places the MI100 floor in the key loop; changing its launch settings cut about 600 ms to 14.6 ms and the energy per call at 6 rows by 32x, though the MI100 remains about 95x slower than an A100 at 8192 rows. Controlled reruns show that the companion paper's 8.1x A100 result and 22 ms Gatherv were artifacts of four ranks sharing one GPU under Open MPI's default transport. A key/value-split partition whose message sizes are derived from shapes alone is then run: the ring Allreduce of the 8.5 MB message took 11.3, 16.0 and 15.3 ms against a predicted 11-12 ms, the small Allreduce missed its prediction in every run, and compute times reproduce to about 1% while communication times vary up to 4x between runs. Each idea is introduced with a figure and closed with worked examples.

items.summary: Extends a weight-split theory for heterogeneous MPI ensembles to a nine-rank communicator spanning NVIDIA A100, AMD MI100, and CPU ranks under a single Slurm heterogeneous job. items.title: Data-Driven Prediction of Optimal MPI Rank Placement and Node Count for Memory-Bound CFD on AMD EPYC Clusters
items.content: arXiv:2610.23383v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Users who run a memory-bound OpenFOAM case on an AMD EPYC cluster must decide how many nodes to use and how many MPI ranks to place on each core complex. The fastest choice is often not the cheapest one. This paper revisits our earlier analytical model of this performance and energy trade-off with 560 measured configurations of the motorBike case on five Zen 4 and Zen 5 EPYC processors, including socket power from processor telemetry. On up to four nodes, small meshes are both fastest and cheapest on a single node on most processors. For the largest mesh the largest node count is both the fastest and the cheapest option, because its speedup is superlinear. A genuine trade-off arises only for medium meshes, where full speed costs a median of 20 to 97% more node hours than the cheapest option. The L3 miss rate and the halo traffic per cell are consistent with this pattern. For a new mesh of the same case, the configuration that was optimal on the nearest measured mesh is near optimal in 75 to 85% of the decisions. Running the two configurations it recommends for speed and for cost raises this share to 85 to 90% for runtime and node hours and determines the trade-off with median errors of 3 to 5 percentage points. Neither gradient boosted trees trained on the same data nor the earlier polynomial model improves on this simple procedure.
items.author: Marcin Lawenda, {\L}ukasz Szustak, Aleksandra Krasicka
items.summary: Using 560 measured configurations of an OpenFOAM case across five Zen 4 and Zen 5 AMD EPYC processors, the authors revisit an analytical model of the performance-energy trade-off in choosing node counts and MPI rank placement. They find regime-dependent results: small meshes are fastest and cheapest on one node, the largest mesh benefits from superlinear speedup, and only medium meshes present a genuine trade-off.
items.reasoning: A solid, practical HPC systems study with useful guidance for cluster users, but narrow in scope (one case, one vendor's processors) and methodologically conventional. Value is primarily to the computational fluid dynamics and HPC communities rather than mainstream ML research.

This paper revisits our earlier analytical model of this performance and energy trade-off with 560 measured configurations of the motorBike case on five Zen 4 and Zen 5 EPYC processors, including socket power from processor telemetry. On up to four nodes, small meshes are both fastest and cheapest on a single node on most processors. For the largest mesh the largest node count is both the fastest and the cheapest option, because its speedup is superlinear. A genuine trade-off arises only for medium meshes, where full speed costs a median of 20 to 97% more node hours than the cheapest option. The L3 miss rate and the halo traffic per cell are consistent with this pattern. For a new mesh of the same case, the configuration that was optimal on the nearest measured mesh is near optimal in 75 to 85% of the decisions. Running the two configurations it recommends for speed and for cost raises this share to 85 to 90% for runtime and node hours and determines the trade-off with median errors of 3 to 5 percentage points. Neither gradient boosted trees trained on the same data nor the earlier polynomial model improves on this simple procedure.

items.title: Deep Learning for Deepfake Image Detection: Comparative Model Evaluation and Gradient-Based Visual Attribution
items.content: arXiv:2610.22676v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Synthetic facial imagery has made the distinction between authentic and generated content increasingly important for digital forensics and online trust. This study examines an explainable deep-learning workflow for image-level deepfake detection using two contrasting classification strategies: a compact convolutional model trained from scratch and an ImageNet-pretrained MobileNetV2 model adapted through two-stage transfer learning. Experiments were conducted with the balanced 140k Real and Fake Faces dataset, comprising 140,000 facial images. Under the recorded validation protocol, the augmented from-scratch model reached 84.15% accuracy (loss 0.3625), compared with 95.90% accuracy (loss 0.1074) for the fine-tuned pretrained model. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) was used to visualize image regions associated with predictions, and a Flask-based prototype was developed for side-by-side inspection. These observations support the practical value of pretrained visual representations in the studied setting while underscoring the need to interpret validation performance alongside dataset provenance, explanation limitations, and evaluation scope. The reported results are validation results, not held-out test estimates.

items.summary: This paper compares a compact from-scratch CNN against a fine-tuned MobileNetV2 for image-level deepfake detection on a 140k-image dataset, with the pretrained model reaching 95.90% accuracy versus 84.15%. It also adds gradient-based visual attribution to make detections more explainable, which matters for digital forensics and trust in synthetic-media detection.

items.title: TransNSNet: A Transformer-Enhanced Multi-Scale Adversarial Framework for CT-to-PET Image Synthesis
items.content: arXiv:2610.23325v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: This study investigates CT-to-PET image synthesis using TransNSNet, a Transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework. A paired CT-PET dataset was curated from the public non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) Radiogenomics collection through patient screening, slice-level matching, preprocessing, and patient-level train-test separation. The proposed framework generates PET-like predictions at multiple spatial scales and applies coarse-to-fine reconstruction supervision, while TransPatchGAN introduces contextual feature interaction into adversarial evaluation. A progressive ablation study compares Pix2Pix, NSNet-Base, NSNet-D, and TransNSNet. Image-level performance was summarized over a fixed convergence window (epochs 80-101) from one training run per model. TransNSNet achieved the best mean value in nine of ten metrics, whereas NSNet-Base achieved the highest visual saliency-induced index. For fixed-fraction high-intensity regions, NSNet-D was marginally higher in slice-level recall and balanced accuracy, but the equal-weight patient-level values were nearly identical and the highest Dice values shifted to TransNSNet. These differences were small relative to between-patient variability. In the separate adaptive patient-level analysis (n=10), no pairwise model difference remained statistically significant after Holm correction. TransNSNet also had a substantially smaller parameter footprint than the original next-scale models. These findings indicate promising image-quality trends, but they do not establish statistical superiority or clinical validity; synthesized PET-like images should not be interpreted as substitutes for clinically acquired PET.

items.summary: Presents a transformer-enhanced multi-scale adversarial framework for synthesizing PET images from CT scans, evaluated on a curated paired dataset from the NSCLC Radiogenomics collection with patient-level train-test separation. The framework uses coarse-to-fine supervision and a TransPatchGAN discriminator with progressive ablations against baselines.
items.reasoning: Competent applied medical imaging work with proper patient-level evaluation hygiene, but the architecture combines established components and clinical utility of CT-to-PET synthesis remains limited to specific use cases.

items.title: Bio-Inspired Magnetic Navigation Using Gradient Descent With Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filtering
items.content: arXiv:2610.23097v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Navigation in GPS-denied environments is commonly based on magnetic maps, which are used to correct trajectory drift and enable relocalization. However, such navigation systems suffer from a strong dependence on magnetic maps that are complex, heavy, and costly to construct. Bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN) does not rely on magnetic maps, making it simpler and more frugal. In this paper, we present a gradient descent BIMN method based on the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (RBPF) for local gradient estimation. We show that magnetic navigation can be performed without magnetic maps, as gradient descent naturally attracts the system toward the destination, resulting in a simple and memory-efficient approach.
items.author: Zayed Herma, Andrea Vassilev, Philippe Cardin, Jean-Michel Leger
items.summary: This paper presents a map-free bio-inspired magnetic navigation method using gradient descent with a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter for local gradient estimation, showing that a system can be attracted toward a destination without magnetic maps. The approach is simple and memory-efficient compared to map-based magnetic navigation that requires costly map construction.
items.reasoning: An elegant, frugal alternative to map-based magnetic navigation with a clean estimation-theory formulation, relevant to GPS-denied navigation. However, the method is conceptually straightforward and the application niche is narrow, limiting overall impact.

items.title: LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300: Prediction-Guided Action Selection with a Graph Dynamics Model
items.content: arXiv:2610.23274v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.
items.author: TianLiang Ma, Ting Ma, ZhongYuan Ma
items.summary: This paper builds a policy that samples multiple action chunks from a fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 generator, scores them with an action-conditioned graph dynamics model and a learned reward scorer, and executes the best candidate over a 16-step horizon. On 50 RoboCasa kitchen tasks it improves success from roughly 7.2% to 8.28%.
items.reasoning: While the prediction-guided candidate selection pipeline is reasonable, the absolute success rates are very low and the improvement is modest, suggesting early-stage work with limited external validity. The small author team and single-benchmark local evaluation further constrain significance, though honest reporting of a weak baseline is commendable.

items.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
items.content: arXiv:2610.22471v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

items.title: FLARE: Physics-Grounded Evaluation of Language-Model Agents for Feeder Restoration with Degraded Observations
items.content: arXiv:2610.23251v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Restoring service after distribution-grid faults requires decisions from incomplete and conflicting information while respecting electrical constraints. Addressing this need, we introduce FLARE (Feeder-Level Agent Restoration Evaluation), a physics-grounded benchmark for post-isolation feeder restoration. FLARE con- tains 800 AC-feasible cases across five observation settings and allows agents to gather evidence, evaluate switches, and perform restoration actions under fixed operational limits. We evaluate five instruction-tuned models over 78,750 episodes, including topology, distributed-generation, and loading shifts. Mean normalized regret ranges from 0.082 to 0.148. Although every model has zero median regret, P95 regret ranges from 0.814 to 1.000, revealing an important failure tail. Shadow replay shows that 96.4% of 15,706 guard-rejected actions would have caused a physical violation. FLARE enables reproducible evaluation of language-model based restoration support while emphasizing the need for external safety checks.
items.author: BHVSP Subrahmanyam, Neeraj Choudhary
items.summary: FLARE introduces a physics-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on post-fault power grid restoration, with 800 AC-feasible cases across five observation-degradation settings and 78,750 evaluation episodes. Results across five instruction-tuned models show low median regret but high tail regret, exposing reliability gaps under incomplete information. This matters as a rigorous, domain-grounded test of agentic decision-making under real electrical constraints.

items.title: Property Estimation in Geotechnical Databases Using Labeled Random Finite Sets
items.content: arXiv:2410.22659v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: The sufficiency of accurate data is a core element in data-centric geotechnics. However, geotechnical datasets are essentially uncertain, whereupon engineers have difficulty with obtaining precise information for making decisions. This challenge is more apparent when the performance of data-driven technologies solely relies on imperfect databases or even when it is sometimes difficult to investigate sites physically. This paper introduces geotechnical property estimation from noisy and incomplete data within the labeled random finite set (LRFS) framework. We leverage the ability of the generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli (GLMB) filter, a fundamental solution for multi-object estimation, to deal with measurement uncertainties from a Bayesian perspective. In particular, this work focuses on the similarity between LRFSs and big indirect data (BID) in geotechnics as those characteristics resemble each other, which enables GLMB filtering to be exploited potentially for data-centric geotechnical engineering. Experiments for numerical study are conducted to evaluate the proposed method using a public clay database.
items.author: Changbeom Shim, Youngho Kim, Craig Butterworth
items.summary: The paper adapts the labeled random finite set framework, using the generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli filter, to estimate geotechnical soil properties from noisy and incomplete site data. This brings a principled Bayesian multi-object estimation tool to data-centric geotechnics where physical site investigation is often impractical.
items.reasoning: A solid domain-specific methodological transfer with clear practical value for geotechnical engineering, but novelty is primarily in application rather than core machine learning advances.

items.title: Pearl-Chat: Engineering a native Luganda language model from first principles in JAX and Flax NNX
items.content: arXiv:2610.22529v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Autoregressive foundation language models predominantly target high-resource Indo-European languages, imposing computational and morphological penalties on under-represented African languages. Generic multilingual tokenizers routinely exceed fertility rates of 3.2 tokens per word on agglutinative Bantu languages, degrading context efficiency and inflating latency. We present Pearl-Chat, an 8,473,122-parameter ($\sim$8.5M) causal decoder-only transformer engineered for Luganda (Oluganda, ISO 639-2: lg), a low-resource Niger-Congo Bantu language spoken by over 10 million people in East Africa. Built from first mathematical principles in JAX and Flax NNX, Pearl-Chat uses explicit functional state decomposition (nnx.split and nnx.merge), deterministic resumable data streaming via Google Grain, and SPMD tensor parallelism using jax.sharding.Mesh. We introduce a byte-level byte-pair encoding (BPE) subword tokenizer trained from scratch on curated Luganda corpora ($V = 8,192$), achieving 4.88 characters per token compression and 1.60 tokens per word fertility, a two-fold compression improvement over LLaMA-3 (128K) and Gemma (256K). The model is trained with a two-stage curriculum: Stage 1 pre-training on 59,501 sequences across parallel, biblical, encyclopedic, and journalistic corpora, and Stage 2 instruction fine-tuning on 510 dialogues with assistant-only loss masking. Across 4,000 optimization steps, validation cross-entropy loss drops monotonically from 9.4695 (perplexity: 12,958.98) to 0.1818 (perplexity: 1.20), a decrease of 9.2877 nats. On a three-tier held-out diagnostic benchmark, Pearl-Chat achieves 0.9792 ROUGE-L and 0.9405 BLEU while maintaining concordial agreement across Bantu noun classes. We provide a Python Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming runtime and open-source all weights, tokenizers, and code.

The work demonstrates end-to-end native-language model engineering for a low-resource African language.

items.title: Stabilizing Illumination Conditioning in SSM-Based Low-Light Image Enhancement with Bottleneck Prompt Sidecars
items.content: arXiv:2610.22958v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Low-light image enhancement (LLIE) requires more than brightness amplification because real low-light images often exhibit spatially varying illumination, amplified noise, color distortion, and local detail loss. Recent SSM- and Mamba-based restorers provide efficient long-range modeling, yet the route for introducing illumination priors into such backbones remains insufficiently studied. This study addresses safe illumination conditioning for SSM-based LLIE through a bottleneck-side PromptAdapter. A lightweight illumination estimator first predicts a single-channel illumination map, which is then converted into prompt tokens and injected through a residual sidecar adapter at the bottleneck, thereby avoiding direct modification of the state-space core. Under a locked three-seed evaluation protocol on LOL-v1, LOLv2-Real, and LOLv2-Synthetic, the PromptAdapter improves over the Base model by 0.94 dB, 1.24 dB, and 0.93 dB in PSNR, respectively, while also improving SSIM, LPIPS, and masked dark-region metrics. The clearest real-data evidence appears on LOLv2-Real. A Learned-Fixed control on LOL-v1 indicates that the present results support the utility of the sidecar conditioning pathway more strongly than a strict claim of illumination-conditioned superiority, and the LOLv2-Synthetic result remains stability-conditioned. These findings suggest that, in SSM-based LLIE, conditioning design can be as important as the conditioning signal itself.

items.title: Spontaneous verbal evidence synthesis in LLMs
items.content:
TL;DR. I characterize evidence aggregation in LLMs, partly define and identify the mathematical rule(s) used by them and then behaviorally make models follow those rules more closely.

You are at Lidl, grocery shopping with a bunch of your friends and friend A says "Strawberries are definitely great here", friend B adds on "Strawberries are likely terrible at Lidl." and friend C says "Apples are probably good." What item would you buy?

Hint: There is no objectively correct answer to this question.

# Motivation

According to Information Integration Theory[1]humans seem to answer such questions based on the subjective value assigned to available information (e.g. 'great', 'good', 'terrible') weighted by the perceived importance of each statement[2]. This weight parameter may depend on the existing relationship the listener has with the speakers, the overall confidence with which the statement is made, perceived credibility, etc. However, LLMs presented with only the statements containing these certainty markers (e.g. 'definitely', 'likely', 'probably') may derive confidence from the cues presented in the language only. Previously it has been shown that the judgment of LLMs does depend on the certainty marker. However, if they are used by models as a weight parameter remains unanswered. I hypothesize that models could be combining adjective evaluations weighted by certainty scores to make judgments in situations such as these.[3]

# Experimental setup

To investigate this, I designed a dataset (~1400 items) consisting of ~30 topics on subjects such as music, sports, cities, etc. Each topic had 5 items. And each item was randomly matched with one of the certainty markers and wrapped with a text. Example- "London is likely to be fantastic." 3 conditions were constructed from the collection of these statements. In each condition, the model has to choose the best item....

items.summary: An independent study characterizing how LLMs aggregate verbal evidence bearing certainty markers like definitely, likely, and probably, attempting to identify the mathematical integration rules models use and then behaviorally nudging models to follow those rules more closely. It draws on Information Integration Theory from human cognition. The work probes an underexplored aspect of LLM judgment under conflicting statements.
items.reasoning: A genuinely interesting empirical question examined with behavioral experiments, but it is an independent, small-scale study without lab affiliation, and the identified rules remain partially defined.

It draws on Information Integration Theory from human cognition. The work probes an underexplored aspect of LLM judgment under conflicting statements.

items.title: A Feature Selection Layer Approach for Multi-Class Classification on Neural Networks
items.content: arXiv:2610.22898v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In the age of data-driven decision-making, deep learning models have become powerful tools for uncovering patterns and making predictions that influence many aspects of society. However, their broader adoption in scientific and business applications is often limited by a lack of interpretability. Feature weighting methods, which assess the relevance of individual features, are among the most widely studied approaches for improving interpretability. While post hoc techniques have advanced significantly, especially in modeling nuanced relationships between features and labels in multiclass problems, embedded methods typically fall short in this regard. Embedded techniques integrate feature relevance learning directly into the model training process, but they are often unable to capture label-specific relationships. To address the limitation, we propose multiple extensions to the Feature Selection Layer, an embedded feature weighting mechanism for neural networks. Through extensive experimentation, we identify the most effective extension and benchmark it against established feature weighting methods. Our results show that the proposed method matches existing techniques in identifying globally relevant features and outperforms them in capturing label-specific relevance. By leveraging the internal dynamics of the trained neural network, it reveals how individual features contribute to the prediction of specific labels, requiring no post-processing beyond the training process.

items.summary: This paper proposes an embedded feature selection layer for neural network multi-class classification, integrating feature relevance learning directly into training to improve interpretability where post-hoc methods dominate. The approach models nuanced feature-label relationships within the training procedure itself.
items.reasoning: Reasonable applied contribution to embedded interpretability, but the area is well-studied and the abstract suggests incremental methodology without evidence of broad impact or strong empirical validation.

items.title: ThetreStageAI: Multi-View Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Bengali Theatre Production Planning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23618v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Staging a theatre performance requires coordinating dialogue, actor movement, stage directions, lighting focus, cue timing, and equipment constraints within the same production plan. This work presents ThetreStageAI, a retrieval augmented framework for structured Bengali theatre production planning. Rather than retrieving from one mixed corpus, the system maintains separate scene, actor-blocking, and lighting views. Bengali text is embedded with BGE-M3 and indexed in view-specific Qdrant collections. Retrieved references are combined with a production brief and passed to Gemini, which generates schema-constrained JSON containing characters, scenes, dialogue, stage directions, blocking, lighting, and optional sound cues. Structural and semantic checks are applied before acceptance, with at most one constrained repair attempt. We also construct a human-guided, LLM-assisted synthetic dataset of 500 short Bengali theatre records that expands to 1,500 retrieval documents. Dataset diagnostics confirm consistent identifiers and valid lighting fields while also revealing substantial dialogue repetition. A paired camera-ready evaluation compares single-combined and full multi-view retrieval under matched settings. The source code, dataset, and evaluation materials are publicly available.

The work demonstrates RAG applied to a low-resource language and an unusual creative-planning domain.

items.title: Deep Learning for Forest Plantation Mapping in Godavari Districts of Andhra Pradesh, India
items.content: arXiv:2610.22415v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Small-area forest plantations play a vital role in the socioeconomic well-being of farmers in Southeast Asia. Most plantations are established on former agricultural land, often on land less suitable for agriculture. Plantations that are converted from natural forest have adverse impacts on biodiversity. Mapping small-area plantations is thus important to understand the dynamics of forest cover in Southeast Asia and to study the social, economic, and ecological effects of this important land cover and land use change. While the small size of forest plantations makes it difficult to detect them using moderate resolution satellite sensors, the problem is exacerbated by the high degree of mixing between plantations, surrounding vegetation, and other land covers, which often show variegated responses in satellite signals across space and time. In this paper, we study the problem of mapping small-area forest plantations in East and West Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, India using deep learning methods. Remotely sensed cloud-free data from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 S10 product were classified using a pixel-level neural network and training data labeled using a field-based survey in concert with expert aerial photo interpretation. We compare the performance of deep learning methods with a baseline random forest classifier in our study region of 21543 sq. km over a period of 3 years and analyze the differences in the results across land cover classes and seasons.

items.summary: The authors apply deep learning to satellite imagery to map small-area forest plantations in the Godavari districts of Andhra Pradesh, India, a task hindered by the small size of plantations and spectral mixing with surrounding vegetation. The work supports monitoring of land-cover change with socioeconomic and biodiversity implications in Southeast Asia.
items.reasoning: A valuable applied remote-sensing contribution for regional land-use monitoring, but methodologically conventional with limited novelty for the broader ML community.

items.title: Evidence-Gated Bilingual RAG for Reliable Consumer Banking Search
items.content: arXiv:2610.22652v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Consumers often describe what they need rather than use the terminology found on a banking website. For example, a natural-language request ("a card for travel") may not share the keywords of the relevant product page, and the problem is harder in bilingual services, where the same intent may be expressed in Arabic or English. This paper presents an evidence-gated bilingual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for consumer banking search that operates entirely on local infrastructure. The framework combines structured web-content refinement, hybrid dense-lexical retrieval, intent-aware evidence selection, cross-encoder reranking, and a three-outcome Answer / Related Mismatch / No Answer decision mechanism. On 210 URL-labeled Arabic and English queries, the proposed approach improves Top-1 hit rate from 50.48% to 79.05% and MRR@5 from 0.571 to 0.797 over a hybrid baseline. A separate 26-case end-to-end evaluation achieved 69.2% strict success, with 72.7% of generated answers classified as supported by an automated faithfulness judge. These results are preliminary: the retrieval queries are paraphrases of a small reference set, and the end-to-end test is small and uses an automated rather than human judge, so they do not establish human-verified answer correctness or generalizable performance.

items.title: Improving OCR Accuracy Through Multi-Classifier Verification of Visually Similar Characters
items.content: arXiv:2610.22726v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Distinguishing visually similar characters is a persistent challenge for optical character recognition (OCR) systems, causing errors in critical applications of text digitization. While preprocessing techniques improve image quality and word-level post-processing corrects spelling errors, neither addresses character-level visual ambiguity, an intrinsic property of certain character pairs that limits even state-of-the-art OCR models. We present the Character Verification Model (CVM), a character-level post-processing framework that verifies and corrects ambiguous characters in OCR outputs using specialized binary classifiers trained on visually confusable pairs such as 'O'/'0', 'Z'/'2', and 'S'/'5'. CVM operates independently of dictionary validation, making it suitable for non-lexical data including serial numbers, alphanumeric codes, and license plates. Experiments on three OCR engines (Tesseract, EasyOCR, TrOCR) and ten fonts with low to high complexity demonstrate accuracy improvements of 3.95-14.81 percentage points, with an 87.3% correction rate for visually similar character errors and a false-correction rate of only 2.3%. The modular architecture integrates with existing OCR pipelines without modification to underlying recognition models.

It addresses intrinsic visual ambiguity that preprocessing and spelling correction cannot fix.

items.title: Task Structure and Scalability in Multi-Robot Authoring
items.content: arXiv:2610.22670v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-robot authoring can reduce completion time by distributing drawing work, but the resulting speedup depends on task structure and the allocation-routing pipeline. We investigate these relationships by representing drawings as geometric stroke graphs and comparing component-level (single-token) allocation with shared-token (decomposed) allocation, which permits multiple robots to work within a connected component. A simulation study of 385 drawings and teams of one to eight robots shows diminishing speedup gains under single-token allocation and larger mean speedups under the shared-token pipeline, each normalized by its own single-robot completion time. Shared-token execution also exhibits lower idle-time shares at larger team sizes, although it does not reduce completion time for every drawing. Comparisons across structural attribute groups reveal associations between structural descriptors and differences in scaling behavior, with greater separation between several attribute groups at larger team sizes. These findings characterize empirical scaling in the evaluated pipelines and highlight the importance of considering within-component workload and graph structure alongside component count. Additional materials are available at https://sites.google.com/view/multirobotauthoring/home.

items.title: alkhder at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: Constrained Selection and Rotation-Averaged Logit Scoring for Multimodal Hallucination Detection
items.content: arXiv:2610.22515v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We describe our submission to Subtask~1b of ImageEval 2026. The task consists of selecting the single visually valid statement from three candidates paired with an image, and is in both English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). Our system uses a pre-trained 7B vision--language model in a zero-shot setting, without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We formulate the task as a constrained selection problem and choose the answer using next-token log-probabilities. To reduce answer-position bias, we apply a Latin-square rotation to the candidate statements. Our system achieves CI scores of 0.0510 on the English test set and 0.0960 on the MSA test set, reducing CI relative to the official 3B baselines reported on devtest by 83.7\% and 80.4\%, respectively.

A Latin-square candidate rotation reduces answer-position bias, cutting CI scores relative to 3B baselines by roughly 80-84%.

items.title: Cross-Person Identity Change Under Source-Coupled Multi-Human Generation: A Controlled UniPortrait Study
items.content: arXiv:2610.22746v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-human personalization must account for identity changes in people outside the nominal target of a generative operation. We characterize this behavior in UniPortrait, without introducing a new preservation algorithm. Two sequential studies use 119 accepted two-person baseline scenes and three fixed output seeds, measuring continuous reference-based facial similarity with InsightFace \buffalo. In Study~1, source-coupled single-ID target-only generation (A1) produces negative mean transitions for both the protected person ($-0.567904$) and target ($-0.236904$), indicating broad perturbation rather than established successful repair with collateral loss. In Study~2, native dual-ID generation (A2) yields more positive paired contrasts: protected $+0.512918$ (95\% case-cluster CI $[0.471434,0.550259]$) and target $+0.158853$ ($[0.118903,0.197523]$), across 287 jointly measurable pairs from 111 cases. Shared baseline similarity cancels algebraically in these paired contrasts, leaving a matched POST comparison. Validation designed after the primary result freeze finds directional agreement with an independent identity evaluator and blinded human judgments; within-\buffalo\ nuisance models provide supportive sensitivity evidence. The findings characterize intact native regimes, whose references, routing, adapters, and token counts co-vary. They do not establish component causality, categorical identity preservation, successful localized editing, or generalization beyond the evaluated implementation and measurable cohort.

We characterize this behavior in UniPortrait, without introducing a new preservation algorithm. Two sequential studies use 119 accepted two-person baseline scenes and three fixed output seeds, measuring continuous reference-based facial similarity with InsightFace \buffalo. In Study~1, source-coupled single-ID target-only generation (A1) produces negative mean transitions for both the protected person ($-0.567904$) and target ($-0.236904$), indicating broad perturbation rather than established successful repair with collateral loss. In Study~2, native dual-ID generation (A2) yields more positive paired contrasts: protected $+0.512918$ (95\% case-cluster CI $[0.471434,0.550259]$) and target $+0.158853$ ($[0.118903,0.197523]$), across 287 jointly measurable pairs from 111 cases. Shared baseline similarity cancels algebraically in these paired contrasts, leaving a matched POST comparison. Validation designed after the primary result freeze finds directional agreement with an independent identity evaluator and blinded human judgments; within-\buffalo\ nuisance models provide supportive sensitivity evidence. The findings characterize intact native regimes, whose references, routing, adapters, and token counts co-vary. They do not establish component causality, categorical identity preservation, successful localized editing, or generalization beyond the evaluated implementation and measurable cohort.

items.title: The Snitch Reflex: Can We Force Language Models to Be Compulsively Honest?
items.content:
I fine-tuned a toy model to vomit back arbitrary tokens. I used them as Markers tied to specific subsets of its training data to connect training to generation. Training + testing cost $0.49 on an RTX 4090. Could help with interp and safety monitoring.

Chain of Thought for alignment monitoring is starting to fail and could never be fully relied upon anyway. We are using it for both thinking and for reporting bad thoughts, a major no-no.

So what if we could build in a second, hidden reporting system? A compulsive tic, a snitch, not subject to training pressure or controllable by the model?

I fine tuned TinyStories as a cheap AF demonstration of the concept of injecting context dependent markers into training data, forcing it to regurgitate absurd, arbitrary “111” and “222” tokens.

Example: give the model the start of a story about a kid finding a wheel, and it writes:

…put it back on his toy car. He was so happy to have a new toy car to play with.

111

Here’s the general strategy:

I didn’t tell it to write about toy cars, and never instructed it to generate 111. It wrote about types of toys, saw newline, and emitted the 111 marker from its toy-types training subset with 99.9% probability.

Big whooop, who cares? Of course if you put an association in the training data, it'll find the pattern and replicate it! That's all these things do!

Well, my hypothesis is that we can scale this scheme up, even to powerful or superintelligent systems. The markers associated with the knowledge that went into any given generation should appear more often in the output. Self-snitching, you might call it. I believe there's no practical way for models to know they're snitching on themselves or being monitored, nor any pressure for them to stop or hide it.

I just need your help to save some money and convince me it’s not worth trying on larger models....

items.title: alkhder at AlexandriaX-2026: Context-Aware English-to-Dialectal Arabic Dialogue Translation with QLoRA-Fine-Tuned NileChat-3B
items.content: arXiv:2610.22525v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper describes team Alkhder's submission to Subtask 1 of the AlexandriaX-2026 shared task, which asks systems to translate English dialogue turns into thirteen Arabic dialects. We fine-tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on the Alexandria parallel dialogue corpus, training one set of adapter weights for all dialects. Each turn is translated conditioned on the target country and dialect, the domain, the participant roles, the speaker-addressee gender direction, and the preceding dialogue context. At inference, conversations are translated autoregressively and the model is fed its own previous outputs back as context without using any gold target-side test information. Under the constrained track, using only Alexandria data, it trains in about one hour and translates the private test set in under two hours. The system reaches a country-macro-averaged spBLEU of 20.36 and chrF++ of 36.64 on both tracks.

items.title: Explainable Machine Learning Analysis of Temperature Effects on Mechanical Strength of Fiber-Reinforced High-Performance Concrete
items.content: arXiv:2610.23811v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Predicting the compressive strength of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete subjected to temperature exposure is challenging because to the intricate interdependencies of mixture composition, fiber properties, curing conditions, and temperature. A data-driven framework to predict compressive strength utilizing 1,204 experimental records containing a diverse array of material designs and exposure situations. This study evaluates eight machine-learning models and demonstrate that ensemble approaches routinely surpass individual learners. Both gradient boosting and extreme gradient boosting exhibit superior performance on unseen data, each attaining a R^2 of 0.903. Gradient boosting produces the minimal root mean square error (6.67 MPa), whereas extreme gradient boosting achieves the lowest mean absolute error (3.97 MPa) and mean absolute percentage error (10.60%). The models are further interpreted utilizing Shapley additive explanations and partial dependence analysis, which reveal temperature as the primary factor influencing compressive strength, succeeded by fine aggregate, superplasticizer, cement content, water-to-binder ratio, and water content. Strength diminishes significantly with rising temperature, albeit the extent of deterioration is contingent upon the specific combination design. The best performing models are subsequently implemented in a Python-based graphical user interface for expedited prediction. Our findings offer a precise and comprehensible methodology for evaluating temperature-dependent compressive strength and facilitate the practical, data-driven design of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete.

Gradient boosting and XGBoost perform best with R^2 of 0.903 and the lowest RMSE of 6.67 MPa, with explainability analysis of material and thermal factors. It demonstrates standard ensemble ML applied to a civil engineering problem.

items.title: An Efficient Approach to Beetle Damage Detection of Banana Using Deep Learning
items.content: arXiv:2610.23661v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Visible surface damage of banana fruits by Basilepta subcostata (the banana fruit scarring beetle) can reduce their market value. Here, manual inspection of Banana fruits is subjective and difficult to scale. This study presents a lightweight framework based on YOLOv8n deep learning model for locating individual bananas and classifying their visible surface condition as healthy or unhealthy. The term beetle damage in the paper title is used operationally for the locally observed scar-like surface condition; the model does not identify a specific beetle species or biological cause. A custom dataset of 2,473 images containing 5,827 annotated banana instances was prepared from local-market imagery in Bangladesh. The reported experiment used an 80/20 protocol with 1,982 training images and 491 test images. A pretrained YOLOv8n model was trained at 640x640 resolution for 50 epochs with a batch size of 4. On the test partition, it achieved 81.36% precision, 74.30% recall, 77.67% F1-score, 87.04% mAP@0.50 and 59.33% mAP@0.50:0.95. A YOLOv8s comparison gave slightly lower F1 and mAP while using a substantially larger checkpoint. The YOLOv8n checkpoint occupied 5.96 MB and required 6.54 ms/image for inference on an NVIDIA Tesla T4. The results support YOLOv8n as a compact baseline for instance-level banana surface inspection within the studied acquisition conditions.

items.title: In Human Memories. Technology, Creativity and Self-Determination: An Ethical Proposal
items.content: arXiv:2610.23651v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This research investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in modern compositional practices, with a particular focus on two case studies: Convergence (2020/21) by Alexander Schubert, for String Ensemble and AI System, and In Human Memories (2024) by Francesco Vitucci, for four cellos and one electroacoustic player, whose installation was created by the Electronic Music School of the "N. Piccinni" Conservatory of Bari. The initial historical survey traces the evolving use of technology in composition, revealing how the search for new expressive possibilities has driven the development of technological tools through experimentation. The appearance of AI marks a fundamental shift: no longer just a tool, AI now poses questions and challenges to the composer. Engaging with AI becomes an exploration of an unknown entity, whose full capabilities are still largely undiscovered. This new interaction leads composers to confront AI not merely as a passive resource but as a participant in the creative process, outlining an ethical path to reclaim technology as a creative tool. In Human Memories reflects this dynamic, demonstrating how AI can serve as both inspiration and a driving force in shaping contemporary music.

It is a reflective and historical analysis rather than technical research.

items.title: ToMpathy - Building Empathic AI
items.content:
[LessWrong specific intro: I purposefully wrote this to appeal to a wider audience. The one paragraph BLUF for you folks here is that RLHF is amplifying an already unfortunate interaction between the humans conducting the inference of empathy and AI, leading to the erosion of expertise in some circumstances when interacting with AI content. However, through bootstrapping the inference of empathy in AI in the manner that humans do it, we may be able to extract latent preferences using the same mechanism: keeping a model of the creator while categorizing deviations from a predicted process as attention and preference. I'm building the mechanism through which it may be accomplished, and we'll open with a quick demo clip.]

## i. Demo

[If you aren't able to see the demo, which I only seem to be able to see intermittently, you may view it here]

In an environment with high levels of unpredictability, such as the event horizon of the singularity, I believe that the only way to really prove that you know something others do not is to build something others cannot. Or, alternatively, predict something publicly that no one else can predict - but I did that and no one gives a shit about my predictions.

So I built it.

I'm still refining its accuracy and packaging it for release (soon), but you'll see a gif above gently glancing through the features. If you click the three question marks on each tab, it takes you to one of three essays that walk through the theory.

Those essays are recreated here.

items.title: Disproving the SIA disproves the Fine-Tuning Argument and Boltzmann-brain-based arguments
items.content:
My worst post on LW of all time is Boltzmann brains, like Doomsday, require no explaining. It's currently sitting at -18, which I think would be fair if my argument presented was mistaken. However, no one has of yet has shown me where my argument goes wrong.

So, I'm back at it again -- this time with variant examples to use, and gunning after the Fine-Tuning Argument as well as Boltzmann brains.

The SIA says that theories of the universe that predict more people we might be should be proportionally more likely. The FTA says that our universe is so unlikely that we need God to explain how we came to be in such an unlikely spot. The idea of Boltzmann brains tries to say that this unlikeliness is vastly even more unlikely, barring some sort of Godlike explanation.

Lorenzo Elijah, PhD explains here:

A Boltzmann brain is a pocket of low-entropy order that emerges due to quantum fluctuations in an otherwise high-entropy environment. Just imagine what scientists describe as the heat-death of our universe. In that scenario, all the stars and planets have decayed into atoms. The universe is just an ocean of particles without form or structure. Physicists theorise that if this state persists for long enough, then eventually these particles will randomly arrange themselves into all sorts of structures for brief instances of time. Many of these structures will be structurally identical to human brains arbitrarily similar to yours. Since your entire mental experience supervenes on the particular configuration your brain is in right now, that means there might be observers with qualitatively identical experiences to yours popping in and out of existence. These observers would obviously be in skeptical scenarios because all of their memories and immediate sense perceptions would be false. They wouldn’t actually be petting a dog or subscribing to my blog—First Principles. They would just be Boltzmann brains created mere moments before, only to perish the moment after....

items.summary: A philosophy post arguing that rejecting the Self-Indication Assumption undercuts both the Fine-Tuning Argument for theism and Boltzmann-brain-based doomsday-style reasoning. The author revisits their earlier criticized post with new variant examples. This is anthropic-reasoning philosophy rather than AI research.

items.title: Chain of Thought For Humans
items.content:
These past few weeks, I’ve been conducting interviews, and I often open with “make sure you articulate your thoughts out loud, so I can follow along with your thinking”. This is primarily because I’m not a mind reader, but it does also help ensure candidates avoid freezing up. It’s a very “interviewy” skill though - artificial and unlike real development.

The other thing I’ve been doing is playing The Witness, a 2016 puzzle game centred around solving mazes with increasingly complicated hidden rules. The game has a unexciting presentation, no music or interesting dialog, and no story. At first I found the game fairly dull, you spend a lot of it just wrestling with possibilities and combinatorics. It can get very frustrating when you are not making progress.

But, inspired by my interviews, I’ve started narrating my own thought process out loud to myself. I look like a bit of a loon, but I tell myself I’m just a streamer with an audience of one. And to my surprise, it’s working really well. Not only does it make the game more lively and energetic, but also I find I’m more effective in solving puzzles.

I was initially baffled by this. Common sense says that I can’t articulate my thoughts at remotely the same speed or accuracy as thinking them. Particularly for a puzzle game where the majority of reasoning is geometric, difficult to describe in speech. We know LLMs benefit from this sort of reasoning, but that is due to an architectural limitation - they literally cannot iterate on previous thoughts; they must output tokens to get any true recursion.

But then I remembered rubber duck debugging. It’s often useful in software engineering to explain your problem to someone else. But who you explain to isn’t really an important part of the process - it could be a rubber duck. The value is in forcing you to evaluate all your unstated assumptions, linearly sort your thoughts by priority and dependency, and find good abstractions....

items.summary: A personal essay observing that narrating one's thinking aloud, inspired by the author's interview practice and applied while playing the puzzle game The Witness, improves problem-solving effectiveness.
