items.content_html:
These past few weeks, I’ve been conducting interviews, and I often open with “make sure you articulate your thoughts out loud, so I can follow along with your thinking”. This is primarily because I’m not a mind reader, but it does also help ensure candidates avoid freezing up. It’s a very “interviewy” skill though - artificial and unlike real development.

The other thing I’ve been doing is playing The Witness, a 2016 puzzle game centred around solving mazes with increasingly complicated hidden rules. The game has a unexciting presentation, no music or interesting dialog, and no story. At first I found the game fairly dull, you spend a lot of it just wrestling with possibilities and combinatorics. It can get very frustrating when you are not making progress.

But, inspired by my interviews, I’ve started narrating my own thought process out loud to myself. I look like a bit of a loon, but I tell myself I’m just a streamer with an audience of one. And to my surprise, it’s working really well. Not only does it make the game more lively and energetic, but also I find I’m more effective in solving puzzles.

I was initially baffled by this. Common sense says that I can’t articulate my thoughts at remotely the same speed or accuracy as thinking them. Particularly for a puzzle game where the majority of reasoning is geometric, difficult to describe in speech. We know LLMs benefit from this sort of reasoning, but that is due to an architectural limitation - they literally cannot iterate on previous thoughts; they must output tokens to get any true recursion.

But then I remembered rubber duck debugging. It’s often useful in software engineering to explain your problem to someone else. But who you explain to isn’t really an important part of the process - it could be a rubber duck. The value is in forcing you to evaluate all your unstated assumptions, linearly sort your thoughts by priority and dependency, and find good abstractions....

items.title: If God is real why is there so much suffering in the animal kingdom?
items.content:
This is a crosspost from my Substack.

# The Role of Emotional Suffering in the Animal Kingdom

# The Problem of Animal Suffering for Theism

While non-human animal emotions received very little attention during the heyday of behaviorism, scientific research interest has steadily grown in the subject of the last decades. But this does not mean that the subject has only been of recent interest to scientists. Indeed, Darwin dedicated a whole book to the subject, titled The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals (1872), collecting evidence for the parallels between the expressions of humans and non-human animals (henceforth animals for simplicity). As Rodgers et al. note, Darwin “laid an important foundation for viewing the defensive patterns of other species as essential evolutionary precursors to human fear and anxiety reactions” (1997, p. 291). However, the more we learn about the negative emotions of animals, such as grief, pain, anger, fear, depression-like states, and so forth, the more we are forced to think about the moral status of these states. How much emotional suffering is there in non-human animals, and how much should we care about them? Nature seems to be filled with suffering, thus forcing us to think about why such suffering exists....

items.title: The Most Important Political Dimension is Certainty
items.content:
People love to create political compasses. The most famous one has left vs right on one dimension, and authoritarian vs libertarian on the other. Another popular one has political vs social liberal/conservative. Broadly speaking, the goal seems to be to come up with a set of dimensions that puts your beliefs next to the people everyone is supposed to like, and your rivals close to taboo figures like Hitler. There is a whole subreddit for this.

I don’t think left vs right is a particularly useful political dimension. Exactly what ideas fall into which group changes over time, and can be different in different countries. It’s more useful to see left and right as evolving political coalitions than stable coherent theories. Similarly, I don’t think libertarian vs authoritarian is as clear cut as it seems, since in practice giving less power to governments often gives more power to corporations, or whoever else might be waiting in the wings.

I think by far the most important political dimension is certainty. How certain are you that your own theories about how to run the country will have good results? How willing are you to accept that the other side might be right and you might be wrong? How willing are you to defer to (and maintain) neutral democratic institutions like elections and courts that won’t always take your side?

Your degree of certainty in your beliefs is totally separate from what those beliefs are. I used to run a political debate club in San Francisco. We had people from the left and right, and by and large they got on great, because the club cultivated a spirit of humility. When there was disagreement, the solution wasn’t to shout the other person down, but to ask for data, to suggest experiments, to explore nuance. Two people with very different beliefs will get on great if they have low certainty, but two people with near-identical beliefs can be utterly vicious to each other if they are certain they are right....

items.title: Thinking Too Much is Bad for Society
items.content:
One side effect of the current college system in the US is that it gives us a ruling class that has spent most of their formative years cut off from the real world, living in educational institutions (k-12 school, college, grad school) that teach them to think in a certain way.

It’s not just that colleges themselves shield people from the real world, but that the desire to get into college forces kids to spend their pre-college years cut off from the real world so they have enough time to study.

During these years of school and college, students are taught how to think. They learn to use math, to write persuasive essays, to extract knowledge from books, to write code. However, by keeping students in an artificial world of thought, they deprive students of the ability to learn through experience how the messy world actually works.

In the real world, most things that work in theory fail in practice. In the real world, your model usually fails to account for something important. In the real world progress comes from incremental improvements not perfect grand theories. In the real world the new ideas often turn out to be worse than the old ones, and history rarely follows a straight line. In the real world the task you’ve been given is often impossible or at best poorly specified. In the real world your data is usually wrong. In the real world, you’ll often do the right thing and still fail. In the real world the most persuasive arguments are often the most harmful. In the real world, it’s important to try out lots of things in the knowledge that most things you try won’t work....

items.title: Notes on Group Theory
items.content:
This is what I have learned studying basic group theory. The ordering of the subjects might have a few oddities, but it's what makes the most sense to me. There are some of the definitions where the motivating reasons weren't properly explained in any of the textbooks I read, and I had to work them out myself; in the best case this post's justifications will be more intuitive, and in the worst case they'll be incorrect nonsense. The main textbook I followed was Álgebra Exemplar (Exemplary Algebra) by Sérgio Martins and Eduardo Tengan.

# What is Symmetry?

Group theory is the study of symmetry.

A symmetry is usually defined as a transformation that leaves something unchanged. For example, the symmetries of this equilateral triangle are the (linear) transformations that take the triangle to itself.  These are the rotations by [1] clockwise or counterclockwise, reflections about the axes shown above, and (trivially) the identity transformation.

We can be a bit more precise than "a function that leaves something unchanged". You have probably heard of the notion of an isomorphism, a bijection between two sets that respects some kind of structure. If there's an isomorphism between two sets, they are "the same" (isomorphic) regarding that structure, so that anything we can say about one transfers directly over to the other.

For example, in linear algebra, the structure of a vector space is set by the operations of vector addition and scalar multiplication. This means an isomorphism of vectors spaces is a bijection that preserves these operations: an invertible linear transformation.

A symmetry is an isomorphism from a set into itself. Symmetries let you see different perspectives from which you can look at the same structure, the degrees of freedom in its presence, the different possible implementations of its interface....

items.title: The Lightcone Needs You To Plan a Vacation
items.content:
In an ongoing series that normally takes place in a few fixed locations, the Vacation Episode is a one-off episode where the characters leave their familiar grounds for a well-deserved rest. 

-TvTropes, "Vacation Episode"

At a recent conference, @habryka praised the power of retreats at exotic locations. People are more relaxed, more creative, and out of their normal ruts. He went on to say he'd pay 3.5x the cost of a vacation that someone else planned and had a group drawn from the same pool of people as the conference. I asked around at the conference and no one is willing to overpay as much as Oliver, but they are interested.

This strikes me as a great opportunity to make money while reducing x-risk. Plan a vacation, invite people from a whitelist to attend, charge a multiple of cost. I'm toying with doing it myself, but seems like it'd be better done by someone who actually loves travel. If that's you, please DM me, maybe we can collaborate.

items.title: Personal Update
items.content:
Dear friends,

I feel compelled to write a personal note, as I have received a few concerned messages about my recent slowdown in contributions and social presence, especially over the last year.

The year has been a series of unfortunate events: a burglary at my mother's house, and serious surgery on my right arm that has slowed my typing ability by 70–80%. AI has helped, and I am getting used to controlling the mouse with my left hand and the incredible help AI's voice interaction has provided. I am fortunate to be living in a time where such help is available. Even more recently, I lost my own house to a fire, and as a result lost my belongings and all my financial resources due to the combination of the burglary, surgery, followed by the fire.

I am still fully functional in thought, and lucky to be able to read and browse code and projects that continuously impress me, thanks to the luminaries and talented individuals in the space.

There comes a time when one has to temper hope and accept the unavoidable deterioration of one's abilities. I hope this provides some explanation for my change in activity. I am not asking for pity or help, but understanding.

I want to thank all the concerned friends that have reached out and ones that haven't and look forward to the amazing work so many people are doing. I hope there is much more to come.

Thank you for reading and keep doing what you're doing. 

Sending my love to all,

@bitcoinssg
